projectTitle: Harborview Health Partners: Real Governance for Claims Data, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of a governed claims lakehouse — Auto Loader, Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, and Unity Catalog row/column security, for one fictional healthcare network, from a shared login with full patient access to real, auditable role-based governance.
businessContext:
**Harborview Health Partners** is a fictional multi-clinic healthcare network: 15 clinics across one metro region, processing insurance claims for roughly 40,000 patients. The problem: all claims data — diagnosis-adjacent billing detail, billed amounts, and full patient identifiers including names and SSNs — sits in one flat legacy export, and every analyst, from billing staff to clinical quality reviewers to compliance auditors, logs into the same shared analytics account with unrestricted access to everything. Compliance has flagged this as a real risk: there is no way to prove who can see what, no way to let clinical reviewers work with claims data without exposing a patient's identity, and no audit trail.

You've been brought in as a Databricks/Lakehouse Engineer to fix this with real governance, not a bigger spreadsheet. This series follows that build end to end — including a real data-quality incident where a deliberately lenient check let bad data reach a financial report, found and fixed in front of the people it affected.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Harborview Health Partners has: a Unity Catalog catalog (`harborview`) with `bronze`/`silver`/`gold` schemas; nightly claims files landed via Databricks Auto Loader into `claims_raw`, append-only with full file-level traceability; a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline building `claims_clean` with built-in data-quality expectations; two Gold tables — a clinic-level `claims_summary_gold` that's safe for broad use by construction, and a patient-level `claims_detail_gold` protected by a real Unity Catalog row filter (restricting non-compliance users to their assigned clinics) and column masks (redacting patient name/SSN for everyone except the compliance group), backed by a `clinic_access_lookup` table and `pii_category` classification tags; Databricks Workflows orchestration; and a real data-quality incident — a lenient "warn" expectation that let malformed claims distort a financial total — found, root-caused, fixed, and permanently monitored. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how Auto Loader, Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, and Unity Catalog governance fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Harborview Health Partners: Why Compliance Can't Tell Who Saw What
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: uncovering why 15 clinics' worth of claims data sits behind one shared login with no way to prove who can see what, before any Unity Catalog object gets created.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll build a governed Lakehouse for a fictional multi-clinic healthcare network, **Harborview Health Partners** — 15 clinics across one metro region, roughly 40,000 patients, and an insurance-claims process that, today, runs entirely on one flat legacy export and one shared analytics login. Billing staff, clinical quality reviewers, and the compliance team all sign into the same account, with the exact same access to everything in that export — diagnosis codes, billed amounts, clinic of service, and every patient's full name and Social Security number.

By the end of this series you'll have landed that same claims data through Databricks Auto Loader, cleaned it with a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline, aggregated it into governed gold tables, and locked it down with Unity Catalog row filters and column masks so each team sees exactly what its job requires — and nothing else. This video starts the same way every real governance project starts: not with a catalog or a table, but with a meeting about who can see what today, and why nobody can currently answer that question with any confidence.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school where every single file cabinet in the office — the one with class schedules, the one with the nurse's private medical notes, the one with family court papers — all opens with the exact same key, and every teacher, the lunch lady, and the hall monitor all carry a copy of that same key. Nobody did anything wrong on purpose. It's just that whoever set up the office years ago made one key because it was simpler, and nobody has gone back to make separate keys since.

That's exactly what's happening at Harborview Health Partners, except the file cabinet is full of real patients' names, medical billing codes, and Social Security numbers, and the people carrying that one shared key are billing staff, nurses who review care quality, and the compliance team whose entire job is making sure nobody peeks at things they shouldn't. Your job is to design a system with separate, provable keys for each group — so people whose work doesn't need a patient's real name never see it, and so there's a written record of who opened which drawer.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of a data-governance engagement, and the symptom that gets you called in — "compliance can't tell who saw what" — is a risk statement, not a requirement. Your job in this first conversation isn't to design anything yet; it's to resist the urge to jump to a fix and instead extract, team by team, exactly what level of access each group's actual job requires, so you can see precisely how far today's access exceeds that need. Minimum-necessary access to protected health information, and the ability to produce an audit trail of who accessed what, are standard practices for organizations handling this kind of data — this series treats them that way throughout, without citing any specific regulation's exact requirements, which is a question for Harborview's own compliance and legal counsel, not for a training series.

At Harborview, discovery surfaces the same pattern you'll see again and again in healthcare data work: the current access model is maximal by accident, not by decision. One flat export, one shared login, three populations with genuinely different needs — and nobody has ever gone back to narrow it, because narrowing access after the fact requires exactly the kind of row- and column-level enforcement this series spends its architecture and implementation lessons building. This lesson's only job is to name the gap precisely enough that the next lesson can turn it into a testable policy.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Before the meeting, write down what you don't actually know

Walk in with the real ambiguities a complaint like "compliance can't tell who saw what" is hiding:

- Who actually needs to see a patient's real name and SSN to do their job, versus who just needs a billing total or a de-identified trend?
- Is there currently any way to prove, after the fact, which specific person looked at a specific patient's record?
- Does every team log in separately today, or is there really one shared account everyone uses?
- What's the actual blast radius if that one shared login's password ever leaked?
- What would "fixed" even look like to the compliance team specifically — a policy document, or something a system actually enforces?

## Step 2 — Run the meeting as an interview, not a listening session

Harborview's Chief Compliance Officer, **Dr. Elena Vasquez**, opens with the kind of sentence that needs follow-up questions: "We have no idea who's been looking at what. Everyone signs into the same `analytics_shared` login, full names and SSNs included, and if we got audited tomorrow, I couldn't tell you who pulled a specific patient's record, or why."

```
Q: Who actually uses that shared login today?
A (Elena): Billing staff reconciling claims, Marcus's clinical quality
           reviewers, and my own compliance team. Three very different
           jobs, one identical level of access.

Q: Marcus, does your clinical quality team actually need patient
   names and SSNs to do quality review?
A (Marcus Chen, Director of Clinical Quality): Almost never. We're
   looking for patterns -- which clinics have denial-rate spikes,
   which diagnosis codes are trending. A patient's identity doesn't
   change that analysis at all.

Q: Priya, what does Finance actually need out of this data?
A (Priya Sharma, VP of Finance): Billed amounts and claim counts by
   clinic, rolled up daily. We've never once needed a patient's name
   to close the books.

Q: Elena, who on your team actually needs full, identifiable records?
A (Elena): A small audit group -- four people, not forty. Everyone
   else touching this data could do their job on de-identified or
   clinic-level numbers and never notice the difference.
```

That last answer is the whole project in one sentence: the current system grants maximum access to everyone because nobody built anything narrower — not because anyone's job actually requires it.

## Step 3 — Write the one-page findings document

```
HARBORVIEW HEALTH PARTNERS -- ACCESS DISCOVERY FINDINGS

Current state: One flat legacy claims export. One shared login
  ("analytics_shared") used by billing, clinical quality, and
  compliance alike. No per-user audit trail. Full patient names and
  SSNs visible to every user, regardless of role.

Who needs what (as stated in discovery, not yet a policy):
  Billing/Finance (Priya's team):   Clinic-level billed amounts,
                                     claim counts, denial rates.
                                     No patient identity needed.
  Clinical Quality (Marcus's team): De-identified diagnosis and
                                     outcome trends, across clinics.
                                     No patient identity needed.
  Compliance audit group (Elena's
    team, ~4 people):               Full patient-level records,
                                     including name and SSN, for
                                     audits -- every access logged to
                                     an individual.

Confirmed risk: no way today to prove who accessed a specific
patient's record, or to prevent clinical quality staff from seeing
SSNs they've never needed.
```

## Step 4 — Circulate it and get explicit confirmation before moving on

Send this findings document to Elena, Marcus, and Priya individually and ask each the same direct question: "Does this match what your team actually needs, and is anything missing?" Their explicit yes is what the next lesson turns into a written, testable access policy — this document only describes the problem; it doesn't yet draw any enforceable lines.

Only Elena's four-person audit group actually needs identifiable records, and there's no per-user audit trail today. I've got a findings doc circulating for sign-off before I turn this into an actual access policy next.

We now know exactly which teams need which level of access, and we're building toward a system that can prove who saw what.

lessons.title: Turning "Lock This Down" Into a Testable Access Policy
lessons.summary: Converting the discovery findings into one precise, testable access policy for claims data — specific enough to later enforce with Unity Catalog row filters and column masks.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 1 gave you real findings: three teams, three very different needs, one shared login. That explains the problem but doesn't fix it. This lesson turns "lock this down" into a written, specific, testable access policy — one that states exactly which columns get masked, for whom, and exactly which rows each role is allowed to see — specific enough that a Unity Catalog row filter or column mask, built later in this series' architecture and implementation lessons, can be checked against it directly.

This policy document is what every later technical decision in this series answers to. The row filter on `claims_detail_gold`, the column mask on `patient_name` and `patient_ssn`, and the data-classification tags applied to sensitive columns all trace back to one clause written in this lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine giving everyone at school a different colored name badge instead of one master key — a red badge for the nurse that opens the medical file drawer, a blue badge for the front office that only opens the attendance drawer, and no badge that opens every drawer except the principal's. But just saying "give people badges" isn't enough — you have to write down, in exact detail, which badge opens which drawer, so whoever makes the badges isn't left guessing.

That's what we're doing now for Harborview — turning "only let the right people see the right things" into an exact, specific list: which badge sees full patient names, which badge sees the data with names blacked out, and which badge only ever sees clinic-level numbers instead of any single patient's record at all.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A policy that sounds reasonable in a meeting and a policy that's actually enforceable are two different artifacts, and the gap between them is where most "we locked it down" projects quietly fail. The test is falsifiability: for every clause, you need a concrete example of a query against a specific role that produces an unambiguous, checkable answer. "Clinical Quality shouldn't see identifying information" is not implementable. "Any query run under the Clinical Quality role returns `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` as NULL, on every row, for every clinic, with zero exceptions" is implementable — and arguable, which is exactly what you want in this meeting, not three weeks into building row filters.

For Harborview specifically, the policy has to resolve three roles against two gold tables: Billing/Finance gets clinic-level aggregates only, with no access to patient-level rows at all; Clinical Quality gets patient-level rows across every clinic for trend analysis, but with identifying columns always masked; and a small Compliance Audit role gets unmasked, patient-level access to any clinic, with every query attributable to one individual rather than a shared account. Writing this down precisely, and getting it signed off by the three people who'll actually be affected by it, is what separates a policy a system can enforce from a policy that only exists as good intentions in a meeting.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Pull every testable claim out of the discovery findings

- Billing/Finance needs clinic-level aggregates only — no patient identity, ever.
- Clinical Quality needs cross-clinic trend data — no patient identity, ever — but needs every clinic, not just one.
- Compliance's audit group (about four people) needs full, identifiable patient-level records, with every access logged to an individual.
- Nobody outside that audit group should ever see a patient's real name or SSN, in any report, under any role.

## Step 2 — Draft the candidate policy and pressure-test it live

```
DRAFT POLICY v1

1. BILLING/FINANCE role: may query clinic-level daily aggregates
   (total billed amount, claim count, denial rate) for any clinic.
   May NOT query patient-level detail rows at all.

2. CLINICAL QUALITY role: may query patient-level detail rows across
   ALL 15 clinics, for diagnosis and outcome trend analysis.
   patient_name and patient_ssn must return NULL for this role, always.

3. COMPLIANCE AUDIT role: may query patient-level detail rows,
   including unmasked patient_name and patient_ssn, for ANY clinic.
   Every query this role runs must be attributable to an individual
   user, not a shared account.

4. ALL OTHER roles/accounts: no access to claims data of any kind.
```

Pressure-test it in the room:

```
Marcus: If my team sees SSNs as NULL, how do we tell two patients
        with the same name apart in a trend report?
You:    You wouldn't need to -- your analysis sits at the diagnosis-
        code and clinic level, not the individual-patient level. A
        case that needs patient-level follow-up is a compliance
        question, not a clinical-quality one.
Priya:  Can my team ever see one clinic's detail rows, not just the
        aggregate, if a number looks wrong?
Elena:  That's a real need, but it's a different role than
        "Billing/Finance" as drafted -- I'd rather log it as a named
        exception request than quietly widen the policy here.
You:    Agreed -- that's a Lesson 3 scoping conversation, not a
        policy change today.
```

## Step 3 — Attach a verification method to every clause

```
Clause 2 verification: A Clinical Quality query against
  claims_detail_gold must return patient_name and patient_ssn as
  NULL on every row, across all 15 clinics, with zero exceptions.

Clause 3 verification: The same query, run under Compliance Audit,
  must return the real values -- and must be traceable to that
  individual user's identity in an access log, not to a shared login.

Clause 1 verification: A Billing/Finance query against
  claims_detail_gold is rejected outright -- that role only ever
  touches claims_summary_gold.
```

## Step 4 — Review it line by line and get an explicit yes

Read each clause aloud to Elena, Marcus, and Priya individually: "does this match what your team needs, yes or no?" This is slower than emailing the document, but it's the point where disagreement should surface — catching one here costs a sentence; catching the same disagreement after row filters are built costs a rebuild.

## Step 5 — Version it, date it, and name what it does not cover yet

Save it as `Harborview_Access_Policy_v1.md`, with the approval date and all three names attached. Note plainly what this policy does not yet decide: it says what each role can see, not which specific people are assigned to which role, and not how the system will technically enforce any of it — that's an architecture question for the lessons ahead, not a policy question for this one.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted the discovery findings into one testable access policy, role by role, with a verification method attached to every clause -- Billing/Finance never touches patient-level rows, Clinical Quality sees patient-level trend data with name and SSN always NULL, and only Compliance's four-person audit role sees unmasked identifiers, with every query attributable to an individual. Got explicit sign-off from Elena, Marcus, and Priya before this goes anywhere near Unity Catalog.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have one written, signed-off access policy instead of a vague instruction to 'lock this down.' Every rule in it has a specific way to check that it's actually being followed, which is what keeps this from turning into an argument once the technical build starts.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned 'restrict access' into a specific, written rule for exactly who can see what, and every person who'll be affected by it has already agreed it's correct. That's what makes the system we build next actually enforceable, not just a policy on paper.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Which Roles, Which Data, What's Deferred
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard, written line around what the first version of Harborview's governed claims platform actually delivers, and logging every other request so it's deferred, not forgotten.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a signed-off access policy covering three roles. That's enough to start architecture planning, but "lock this down" surfaced more requests than the policy addresses — Priya's occasional need for one clinic's detail rows, a question about new clinics Harborview might acquire, and more. This lesson draws a hard written line around what v1 of the governed claims platform actually delivers, and logs every other request so it's deferred, not forgotten.

This scope document is what you point back to a few lessons from now, when the build is underway and someone asks for "just one more exception" to the access policy that would quietly expand a tightly-scoped governance project into an open-ended one.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're finally reorganizing a messy closet so everyone can find their own stuff. While you're in there, people keep calling out other things they want fixed too — "can you also alphabetize the garage," "can you add a lock to the shed." Good ideas, but if you try to do all of them this weekend, the closet — the thing that was actually urgent — never gets finished.

The smart move is two lists: what's getting fixed this weekend, and what's on the list for next time. That's exactly what we're doing with Harborview's claims data — deciding exactly which roles and which data get locked down first, and writing everything else down for later instead of trying to fix it all at once.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope management on a compliance-driven rebuild has a specific failure mode to guard against: once stakeholders see one access problem taken seriously, more good ideas for "while you're in there" surface immediately, and each one deserves a real answer, not a reflexive no. The discipline is separating foundation work — the three roles and the row/column enforcement the Lesson 2 policy already defines — from extension work that depends on a foundation that doesn't exist yet, like sharing de-identified data with an outside auditor, or enriching claims with clinical records from a different source system entirely.

For Harborview, v1 needs to ship the one existing claims source, the three roles exactly as policy-defined, enforcement that already keys off clinic identity so it holds up if Harborview adds a 16th clinic, and a real per-user audit trail that finally retires the shared login. Everything else — a fourth role for Finance's occasional exception, external data sharing, EHR enrichment, self-service role management for Elena's team — gets an explicit disposition instead of a shrug, because a request that's silently dropped resurfaces later as a surprise, and surprises are exactly what erode the trust a governance project is supposed to build.

Attach this scope statement to the Lesson 2 policy and ask Elena, Marcus, and Priya for one explicit confirmation covering both documents together. lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: Unity Catalog Governance, Not Just a Shared Login
lessons.summary: Why the fix is a governed Databricks Lakehouse on Unity Catalog, not another filtered export or a hand-maintained list of who's allowed to see what.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With v1 scoped, this is the first real architecture decision: what actually gets built to enforce the Lesson 2 policy. The tempting, cheapest-looking fix is the one Harborview has effectively tried for years — keep the one flat export, hand out a few more logins, and ask people nicely to only look at what they need. This lesson explains why that approach cannot actually satisfy the policy you got signed off on, and why the real fix is a governed Databricks Lakehouse on Unity Catalog: a `harborview` catalog with `bronze`, `silver`, and `gold` schemas, where access control is enforced by the platform itself, not by a login convention.

This is also where the medallion shape gets named for the first time: `harborview.bronze.claims_raw`, landed untouched from the nightly clinic CSV drops; `harborview.silver.claims_clean`, built with a quality-checked transformation step; and two gold tables — `harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold` for the clinic-level numbers Finance and leadership need, and `harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold` for the patient-level records only the Compliance Audit role is allowed to see unmasked. The actual row filters and column masks get built in later lessons — this lesson is about choosing the platform that makes them possible at all.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine that instead of giving everyone a different key to different drawers, you install one smart lock on the whole filing cabinet — a lock that actually checks who's trying to open it, every single time, and writes down exactly who opened it and when. That's very different from just trusting people to only open the drawer they're supposed to, which is basically what Harborview has been doing with its one shared login.

We're picking that kind of smart-lock system for Harborview: one organized digital filing cabinet, with a raw section, a cleaned-up section, and a finished section, and one gatekeeper built into the system itself that checks every person's badge before showing them anything — instead of hoping everyone follows the rules on their own.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scaling access control through convention — a separate filtered export per team, a separate login per role, a spreadsheet somewhere tracking who's supposed to see what — is exactly the ungoverned pattern that produced Harborview's original risk. It has no enforcement mechanism, no audit trail tied to an individual query, and it silently drifts out of sync with the Lesson 2 policy the moment anyone forgets to update a view or rotate a shared password.

A Databricks Lakehouse governed by Unity Catalog solves this differently: one three-level namespace (`catalog.schema.table`) gives Harborview exactly the `harborview.bronze` / `harborview.silver` / `harborview.gold` structure this series needs, with Auto Loader incrementally landing each night's CSV drops into `claims_raw`, a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline applying a declared data-quality expectation on the way to `claims_clean`, and Unity Catalog's row filters, column masks, and data-classification tags available as the actual enforcement mechanism for the policy — built in the architecture and implementation lessons ahead, not this one. This kind of platform-enforced, row- and column-level access control over protected health information is standard practice for organizations in this position; exactly what a given regulation requires of Harborview specifically is a question for its own compliance and legal counsel, not a claim this series makes.

None of this is a new engine for you — it's the same medallion architecture and Unity Catalog fundamentals from `azure-databricks-and-delta-lake` and `advanced-databricks-specialization` earlier in this learning path, applied to one real governance problem instead of a tutorial dataset. This series builds toward the kind of platform judgment the DP-750 certification track is meant to recognize, though nothing here should be read as a guarantee of what that exam specifically covers.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — List the actual constraints before naming a tool

```
CONSTRAINTS:
  - Claims arrive once a night, per clinic, as a CSV drop -- a batch
    problem, not a streaming one, for v1
  - Three roles from the Lesson 2 policy need enforcement at the row
    and column level, not just "please don't open this file"
  - Every Compliance Audit access must trace to an individual, not a
    shared account -- ruling out analytics_shared as a permanent fix
  - 15 clinics today, more possibly later -- enforcement needs to key
    off clinic identity, not a hand-maintained list
  - The team already has Databricks and Delta Lake fundamentals from
    earlier in this path; this is governance applied to that
    foundation, not a new engine to learn
```

## Step 2 — Assign one layer per responsibility

```
LAYER                 OBJECT                        RESPONSIBLE FOR
Raw landing (bronze)  harborview.bronze.claims_raw   Nightly CSV drops via
                                                      Auto Loader, append-
                                                      only, no business logic
Cleaned (silver)      harborview.silver.claims_clean A Lakeflow Declarative
                                                      Pipeline enforcing a
                                                      quality expectation:
                                                      claim_amount_usd > 0
                                                      and valid, non-null
                                                      clinic_id
Clinic-level (gold)   harborview.gold.               Daily aggregate: total
                       claims_summary_gold            billed, claim count,
                                                      denial rate -- what
                                                      Finance and leadership
                                                      query
Patient-level (gold)  harborview.gold.               Access-restricted
                       claims_detail_gold             detail -- what
                                                      compliance audits
                                                      against
Governance            Unity Catalog                  Enforces the policy:
                                                      row filters, column
                                                      masks, classification
                                                      tags (built later)
```

## Step 3 — Name the alternatives considered, and why they lose

```
- A few more shared logins, one per team, each pointed at a filtered
  copy of the export: rejected. Still no per-user audit trail, and
  every new hire or policy change means rebuilding another filtered
  copy that can quietly drift out of sync with the policy.
- Database views with manually granted permissions, no catalog-level
  governance: considered, rejected for v1 -- permissions on a handful
  of views, maintained by hand, don't scale cleanly to 15 clinics
  today and more later, and give no single place to audit access.
- Filtering patient data inside the BI/reporting tool instead of the
  data platform: rejected -- that puts the policy inside a dashboard
  definition, so a second report built against the same tables could
  quietly bypass it.
```

## Step 4 — Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

```
"We're landing claims data through a standard bronze/silver/gold
Lakehouse on Databricks, governed end to end by Unity Catalog, because
the Lesson 2 access policy needs to be enforced by the platform itself
-- at the row and column level, tied to an individual's identity --
not maintained by hand across a growing pile of filtered exports and
shared logins. This builds directly on the medallion architecture and
Unity Catalog fundamentals from earlier in this learning path; nothing
here is a new engine, just governance applied properly to it."
```

## Step 5 — Name what this decision does not require yet

```
THIS DECISION DOES NOT REQUIRE, FOR V1:
  - Real-time or streaming ingestion -- claims still land as a
    nightly batch
  - The actual row filters and column masks to be built yet -- that's
    architecture made possible here, implemented in the lessons ahead
  - Any change to how clinics export their claims files today
  - A decision about the deferred items from Lesson 3 -- this catalog
    structure can support them later without a redesign, but v1
    doesn't build them
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the architecture: a harborview catalog in Unity Catalog with bronze/silver/gold schemas -- claims_raw landed via Auto Loader, claims_clean built as a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline with a data-quality expectation on claim_amount_usd and clinic_id, and two gold tables split by audience: a clinic-level aggregate and a patient-level detail table. Unity Catalog's row filters and column masks are what will enforce the Lesson 2 policy -- rejected more shared logins or hand-maintained view permissions, since neither gives a real per-user audit trail or scales past 15 clinics cleanly.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We're not building anything exotic -- this is the same Databricks and Delta Lake foundation from earlier in the learning path, with real governance applied on top through Unity Catalog instead of more shared logins or manually managed permissions. That's what lets the access policy actually get enforced by the system, not just agreed to on paper.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're not asking Harborview to change how clinics send their claims files, and we're not building something that needs constant manual upkeep to stay secure. We're organizing the data into a governed system that can prove, automatically, who's allowed to see what -- which is exactly the gap Compliance flagged.

lessons.title: Designing the Medallion Layers for Claims Data
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding the Bronze/Silver/Gold layers for Harborview's claims data -- the grain of each one, and why the patient-level gold table needs protection the clinic-level summary doesn't.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Unity Catalog governance chosen as the stack in the last lesson, this is the first architecture-planning session aimed at Harborview's actual data: the medallion layering for claims. We're whiteboarding three layers inside the `harborview` catalog -- **bronze** (`harborview.bronze.claims_raw`, the claims exactly as they land from the clinics' nightly CSV drops), **silver** (`harborview.silver.claims_clean`, validated and de-duplicated), and **gold** (two separate tables, `harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold` and `harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold`, built for two different audiences) -- before creating a single schema.

Nothing gets provisioned in this lesson. The point is to decide, on paper, the grain of each table and which ones actually carry the patient-identifying risk that got Harborview into trouble in the first place with one shared login. Get that boundary right here, and the row filters and column masks planned in the next lesson have an obvious, narrow target. Get it wrong, and Harborview ends up protecting the wrong table -- or protecting all of them equally, which defeats the point of a summary table anyone on the clinical or finance side should be able to query freely.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a hospital kitchen. Raw groceries come in through the back door exactly as the delivery truck dropped them off -- nothing sorted, nothing checked. Then a prep cook cleans and checks everything: throws out anything spoiled, labels it properly. From there, two different things happen. A big pot of soup gets made and ladled out by the bowl -- nobody can tell whose vegetables ended up in whose bowl, so anyone in the cafeteria can grab one. But a special tray gets made up with one patient's name on it, for one specific room -- and that tray has to go through a nurse who checks the room number before it's handed over.

That's the whole plan in this video. The claims data comes in raw, gets cleaned once, and then splits into a "soup" table that's already safe for almost anyone to see, and a "named tray" table that absolutely is not.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the standard medallion pattern -- bronze, silver, gold -- but the planning decision that actually matters for Harborview isn't the layer count, it's where personally identifiable and protected health information (PHI) stops being incidental and starts being the defining risk of a table. Bronze (`claims_raw`) is a direct, append-only landing of the clinics' CSV exports: one row per raw claim line exactly as Auto Loader ingested it, schema-inferred and evolved automatically, with zero business logic and zero filtering -- if a clinic's export has a malformed row, it lands here anyway, because bronze's whole job is being an honest, replayable copy of what actually arrived.

Silver (`claims_clean`) is where a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline applies the first real business logic: deduplication, type casting, and one data-quality expectation enforcing `claim_amount_usd > 0` with a valid, non-null `clinic_id`. It's still grain-identical to bronze -- one row per claim -- just validated.

Gold is where the real architectural fork happens, and it's the one worth whiteboarding carefully. `claims_summary_gold` aggregates to clinic-and-day grain -- total billed, claim count, denial rate -- and in doing so it structurally cannot expose any single patient's record; aggregation itself is a form of de-identification, which is exactly why this table can be queried broadly by finance and operations without row filters or column masks doing any real work. `claims_detail_gold` keeps patient-level grain specifically because clinical and compliance use cases genuinely need an individual claim tied to an individual patient -- and that's precisely the table that inherits every bit of the governance risk the shared-login problem created. Naming that distinction out loud now, before any SQL exists, is what keeps the next lesson's row-filter and column-mask design narrowly scoped to the one table that actually needs it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the grain of each layer before naming a column

```
BRONZE  harborview.bronze.claims_raw
  Grain: one row per raw claim line, exactly as it arrived in a
  clinic's nightly CSV drop. Append-only. No dedup, no validation.

SILVER  harborview.silver.claims_clean
  Grain: one row per valid claim line, after dedup and the
  claim_amount_usd / clinic_id data-quality checks. Still one row
  per claim -- silver cleans, it does not aggregate.

GOLD    harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
  Grain: one row per clinic, per calendar day. Aggregated -- total
  billed amount, claim count, denial rate. No patient-level columns
  exist in this table at all.

GOLD    harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
  Grain: one row per claim, carrying patient_name, patient_ssn,
  clinic_id, claim_amount_usd, and claim status. This is the only
  table in the whole lakehouse where a named human and a dollar
  amount sit in the same row.
```

## Step 2 — Sketch Bronze: what Auto Loader actually hands you

```
harborview.bronze.claims_raw (shape, not yet created)
  clinic_id          STRING    -- inferred from CSV, not yet validated
  patient_name        STRING
  patient_ssn          STRING
  claim_id              STRING
  claim_amount_usd        STRING  -- Auto Loader infers loosely; a
                                      stray "$1,204.00" lands as text
  service_date            STRING
  claim_status             STRING
  _rescued_data             STRING -- Auto Loader's catch-all for any
                                       column it couldn't reconcile
  _source_file              STRING
  _ingested_at                TIMESTAMP
```

Bronze intentionally stores everything as loosely-typed text plus Auto Loader's own `_rescued_data` column. That's not sloppiness -- it's the same philosophy as every other landing zone in this catalog: a malformed row from one clinic's billing export should land successfully and get caught deliberately in silver, not reject an entire night's file.

## Step 3 — Sketch Silver: where the first real decision gets made

```
harborview.silver.claims_clean
  clinic_id          STRING    NOT NULL   -- expectation enforced
  patient_name        STRING
  patient_ssn          STRING
  claim_id              STRING    NOT NULL
  claim_amount_usd        DECIMAL(10,2)   -- cast, and expectation:
                                              claim_amount_usd > 0
  service_date            DATE
  claim_status             STRING
  _silver_loaded_at          TIMESTAMP
```

Silver still carries `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` -- cleaning the data doesn't remove the risk, it just makes the data trustworthy enough to build on. That risk doesn't get handled until the two gold tables are built from this one.

## Step 4 — Sketch Gold and make the governance fork explicit

```
harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
  clinic_id          STRING
  summary_date         DATE
  total_billed_usd        DECIMAL(12,2)
  claim_count               INT
  denied_claim_count          INT
  denial_rate                  DECIMAL(5,4)
  -- no patient_name, no patient_ssn, no claim_id -- structurally
  -- impossible to re-identify a single patient from this table

harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
  claim_id          STRING
  clinic_id           STRING
  patient_name          STRING   -- row filter + column mask target
  patient_ssn             STRING   -- row filter + column mask target
  claim_amount_usd           DECIMAL(10,2)
  claim_status                 STRING
  service_date                   DATE
```

## Step 5 — Name who queries which table, and why that settles the governance question

```
claims_summary_gold  -- Finance, clinic operations leadership, anyone
                        building a dashboard. Broad read access is
                        fine because the table itself can't leak a
                        patient's identity.

claims_detail_gold   -- Billing analysts resolving a specific denied
                        claim, clinical quality reviewing a specific
                        patient encounter, compliance auditing. Every
                        one of these users needs row-level and
                        column-level protection, which the next
                        lesson designs.
```

## Step 6 — Write the one rule this whole series' governance work hangs on

```
RULE: a table only needs row filters and column masks if a single
row in it can be tied back to a named, identifiable patient.
claims_raw and claims_clean carry that risk but are never queried
directly by end users. claims_detail_gold carries that risk AND is
queried directly -- that's the one table protection has to be
airtight on. claims_summary_gold carries no row-level patient risk
at all, by construction, which is why it's the table anyone can be
handed without a single row filter.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Whiteboarded the medallion layers for claims before creating any schema: bronze (claims_raw) lands the nightly CSV drops untouched, silver (claims_clean) applies dedup and the claim_amount_usd/clinic_id data-quality checks, and gold forks into an aggregated clinic-day summary with no patient columns at all versus a patient-level detail table that inherits every bit of PHI risk. That fork is what scopes the row-filter and column-mask work in the next lesson to exactly one table.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We mapped out how claims data will move through the new platform before building anything -- four tables, and a clear line between the one table almost anyone can see (the clinic-level summary) and the one table that needs real access controls (the patient-level detail). That boundary is what keeps the security work in the next step focused instead of applied everywhere by default.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned exactly how claims data will be organized once it leaves the shared login behind -- including a clear split between a summary view your finance and operations teams can use freely, and a detail view that carries patient names and will get real, auditable access controls. That split is the structural fix for the access problem you brought us in for.

lessons.title: Planning Row-Level Security and Column Masking Before Writing a Policy
lessons.summary: Designing the real row-filter and column-mask logic for claims_detail_gold -- which Unity Catalog groups exist, what each can see, and the clinic-access lookup table the policies will query -- before a single CREATE FUNCTION statement runs.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 5 drew a hard line: `claims_detail_gold` is the one table in this lakehouse that carries patient-identifying risk and gets queried directly. This lesson designs exactly how that table gets protected -- which Unity Catalog groups exist, what each group is allowed to see, and the actual lookup logic a row filter and a column mask will need to query at runtime -- entirely on paper, before any `CREATE FUNCTION` or `ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER` statement gets written.

Planning this now, rather than writing the SQL first and reverse-engineering the rule from it, is what keeps the eventual policy auditable: anyone reviewing this design later should be able to answer "who can see what, and why" without reading a single line of SQL.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a filing cabinet with folders for every single patient at every clinic. Right now, anyone with the one shared key can open any drawer and read any folder, name included. What we're planning here is a new set of rules for who gets which key, before the locksmith even starts cutting keys.

The compliance officer gets a master key that opens every drawer, full names and all -- that's their job. A billing clerk gets a key that only opens the drawers for their own clinic, and even then, when they open a folder, the patient's name and ID number are covered with a sticky note -- they can see the claim, not the person. We're drawing that whole key chart on paper first, so the locksmith who builds the actual locks later knows exactly what to cut.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Unity Catalog enforces exactly two primitives here -- a row filter (a SQL function returning a boolean, applied to every row a query touches) and a column mask (a SQL function that transforms a column's value based on the querying user, most often to NULL) -- and the entire design problem is deciding what those two functions need to know before writing either one. That means defining the groups first.

Three Unity Catalog groups cover Harborview's real access needs: `compliance_team` (sees every row, unmasked, for audits and regulatory reporting -- the one explicit exception the backbone calls for), `clinical_quality` (clinic-restricted, PII masked -- reviews claims for care-quality patterns without needing a patient's name), and `billing_analysts` (clinic-restricted, PII masked -- resolves denied or disputed claims for their own clinic). Only `compliance_team` bypasses both protections; the other two groups are structurally identical in what they're restricted from, differing only in which clinic's rows and which business question they're there to answer.

The row filter's logic depends on a lookup table, not a hardcoded clinic list, because clinic assignments change as staff move between Harborview's 15 locations: a mapping table of `user_email` to `clinic_id`, checked at query time against `current_user()`. The column mask's logic is simpler -- a single `IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('compliance_team')` check -- but just as important to design explicitly, because a mask that's even slightly too permissive defeats the entire point of building it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Name the groups and what each one is for

```
compliance_team    -- Regulatory/compliance staff. Needs every row,
                       every clinic, unmasked patient_name and
                       patient_ssn, for audits and regulatory
                       reporting. The one explicit exception.

clinical_quality   -- Clinical quality reviewers. Needs claim and
                       encounter detail for THEIR assigned clinic(s)
                       only, to review care-quality patterns. Does
                       NOT need the patient's name or SSN to do this
                       job -- a claim_id and clinic_id are enough.

billing_analysts   -- Billing/denials staff. Needs claim detail for
                       THEIR assigned clinic(s) only, to resolve
                       denied or disputed claims. Also does not need
                       the patient's identity, just the claim.
```

## Step 2 — Write the access matrix before writing any SQL

```
GROUP              ROW ACCESS            patient_name / patient_ssn
compliance_team    All 15 clinics        Unmasked
clinical_quality    Assigned clinic(s)     Masked to NULL
billing_analysts     Assigned clinic(s)      Masked to NULL
```

## Step 3 — Design the lookup table the row filter will query

```sql
-- Design spec -- built for real once Unity Catalog exists (Lesson 8
-- provisions the catalog/schemas/groups; this table and the
-- functions below are built in a later implementation lesson)
CREATE TABLE harborview.gold.clinic_access_lookup (
    user_email   STRING,
    clinic_id    STRING,
    granted_by   STRING,
    granted_at   TIMESTAMP
);
```

One row per (user, clinic) pair they're allowed to see. A billing analyst covering two clinics gets two rows; a compliance team member doesn't need a row here at all, since their access is handled by group membership, not this table.

## Step 4 — Design the row filter function's logic

```sql
-- Design spec for the row filter (built in a later lesson)
CREATE FUNCTION harborview.gold.clinic_row_filter(clinic_id STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN
  IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('compliance_team')
  OR EXISTS (
       SELECT 1 FROM harborview.gold.clinic_access_lookup m
       WHERE m.user_email = current_user()
         AND m.clinic_id = clinic_row_filter.clinic_id
     );
```

Applied later as `ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold SET ROW FILTER harborview.gold.clinic_row_filter ON (clinic_id);` -- every query against the table runs this function per row, invisibly to the person running the query.

## Step 5 — Design the column mask functions

```sql
-- Design spec for the two column masks (built in a later lesson)
CREATE FUNCTION harborview.gold.mask_patient_name(patient_name STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE WHEN IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('compliance_team')
            THEN patient_name ELSE NULL END;

CREATE FUNCTION harborview.gold.mask_patient_ssn(patient_ssn STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE WHEN IS_ACCOUNT_GROUP_MEMBER('compliance_team')
            THEN patient_ssn ELSE NULL END;
```

## Step 6 — Decide the data classification tags now, so the masks have a target

```
pii_category = 'phi'   -- applied to claims_detail_gold.patient_name
                           and claims_detail_gold.patient_ssn

This tag is metadata, not enforcement -- it's what makes these two
columns discoverable as sensitive in Unity Catalog's lineage and
search, independent of whether the mask is correctly applied. Both
the tag and the mask get applied together; neither one alone is the
control.
```

## Step 7 — Pressure-test the design against a real scenario before moving on

```
SCENARIO: A billing analyst assigned to Clinic 004 queries
claims_detail_gold filtered to claim_id = 'C-88213', which belongs
to Clinic 009.

EXPECTED: Zero rows returned -- the row filter excludes it before
the analyst ever sees a masked or unmasked value. This is the
correct failure mode: silently absent, not visibly denied, which
avoids confirming to an unauthorized user that the claim exists at
all.
```

That's the full behavior this lesson needs to lock down before Lesson 8 provisions the groups these rules depend on.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Designed the row filter and column mask logic for claims_detail_gold before writing any SQL: three Unity Catalog groups (compliance_team, clinical_quality, billing_analysts), a clinic_access_lookup lookup table driving the row filter, and two column mask functions that redact patient_name/patient_ssn to NULL for everyone except compliance. Also locked the pii_category='phi' tag these columns get classified under.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've worked out exactly who sees what in the new patient-level table, and how the system will enforce it -- before any policy gets written. That means when we build this for real, it's implementing an agreed design, not improvising rules under deadline pressure.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've designed exactly who gets to see a patient's name on a claim record and who doesn't -- a compliance team that needs full access for audits, and clinical and billing staff who get the claim detail they need for their own clinic without the patient's identity attached. That's the real fix for the shared-login problem, not just a password change.

lessons.title: Planning the Auto Loader Ingestion Path for Nightly Claims Files
lessons.summary: Mapping where the clinics' nightly claims CSVs land, how Auto Loader will infer and evolve their schema, and the realistic latency target for claims_raw being ready -- before configuring a single stream.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The medallion layers are designed (Lesson 5) and the governance model for the sensitive gold table is designed (Lesson 6). Neither has anything to run against, because nothing has landed in `harborview.bronze.claims_raw` yet. This lesson plans exactly how it gets there: the cloud storage location the 15 clinics' legacy billing systems drop a nightly CSV export into, how Databricks Auto Loader will discover and ingest those files, how its schema inference and evolution behavior needs to be configured given that clinics' exports won't always match column-for-column, and a realistic file-arrival schedule worked out backward from when anyone actually needs the data.

This is the last planning lesson before anything gets provisioned -- the Auto Loader configuration sketched here becomes the literal pipeline code built once the catalog exists.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture 15 different mailrooms, each one dropping off a stack of papers at the same big mailbox outside your building every night, and nobody tells you exactly what time or exactly how each stack will be organized -- one mailroom staples theirs, another doesn't, one of them sometimes adds an extra sheet nobody asked for. Before you build the machine that sorts all this mail every morning, you need to plan for it to handle all of that mess automatically: notice when a new stack shows up, notice when someone added an extra sheet and adjust instead of jamming, and finish sorting with enough time to spare before the office opens.

That's what this lesson plans -- not the sorting machine itself yet, just exactly where the mailbox sits and exactly how the machine needs to behave when it checks it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Auto Loader's whole value proposition is handling exactly the kind of inconsistency 15 independently-run clinic billing systems will produce, but that only works if its schema inference and evolution behavior is configured deliberately rather than left on defaults. The plan: a dedicated cloud storage location -- one container, one folder per clinic, so a malformed drop from one clinic never blocks the other 14 -- that each clinic's legacy system writes a CSV export into once nightly, after its own end-of-day batch close.

Auto Loader's `cloudFiles` source watches that location, incrementally processing only newly-arrived files rather than rescanning everything, and its schema is tracked in a schema location separate from the data itself so schema history survives even if a table gets rebuilt. Because the 15 clinics' exports won't always carry identical columns -- one clinic's system might add a new field a different system never had -- schema evolution is set to add new columns automatically rather than fail the stream, which matches the backbone's append-only, no-business-logic philosophy for bronze: a new column should land successfully and get decided about in silver, not block the whole night's ingestion.

The last planning decision is the schedule, worked backward from when clinical and billing staff actually open a dashboard: clinics' nightly batch exports finish by roughly 11pm local time across all 15 locations, Auto Loader is scheduled to trigger shortly after 1am with a deliberate buffer, and the full bronze-to-silver-to-gold run needs to complete well before a 7am open -- the same backward-planning discipline as any nightly batch pipeline.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide the landing location and its folder structure

```
Storage account: harborviewdatalake (ADLS Gen2)
Container:        claims-landing
Path convention:  claims-landing/<clinic_id>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/claims_export.csv

abfss://claims-landing@harborviewdatalake.dfs.core.windows.net/
  clinic-001/2026/10/23/claims_export.csv
  clinic-002/2026/10/23/claims_export.csv
  ...
  clinic-015/2026/10/23/claims_export.csv
```

One subfolder per clinic, not one shared folder for all 15 -- so a malformed file from one clinic's legacy system is isolated to that clinic's path and never blocks the other 14 from ingesting on schedule.

## Step 2 — Plan the Auto Loader read, and where its schema gets tracked

```python
# Design sketch -- the stream this becomes once the catalog exists
raw_df = (
    spark.readStream
         .format("cloudFiles")
         .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")
         .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation",
                 "abfss://claims-landing@harborviewdatalake.dfs.core.windows.net/_schema/claims_raw/")
         .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns")
         .option("header", "true")
         .load("abfss://claims-landing@harborviewdatalake.dfs.core.windows.net/")
)
```

`cloudFiles.schemaLocation` is a path Auto Loader owns to persist the schema it has inferred so far -- separate from the data itself, so the schema's history survives even across a full table rebuild.

## Step 3 — Decide the schema evolution behavior deliberately, not by default

```
MODE CHOSEN: addNewColumns

A clinic's billing system adding a new column mid-year (say, a new
"adjustment_code" field) should not fail the nightly stream for that
clinic or any other. addNewColumns lets the new column land in
claims_raw automatically and triggers a stream restart to pick up
the new schema -- the raw layer absorbs the surprise; silver is
where a decision gets made about whether that new column matters.

MODE REJECTED: failOnNewColumns -- would halt ingestion the first
night any one of 15 independently-run clinic systems changes its
export format, which given 15 separate legacy systems is a matter
of when, not if.
```

## Step 4 — Plan the file-arrival schedule backward from when staff open a dashboard

```
~11:00pm  -- Last of the 15 clinics' legacy billing systems finishes
             its nightly batch close and writes its CSV export
 1:00am   -- Auto Loader job triggers (2-hour buffer already built in
             past the latest expected clinic export)
 1:20am   -- All 15 clinics' files discovered and ingested into
             claims_raw
 1:35am   -- Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline run produces claims_clean
 2:00am   -- Gold tables refresh
 7:00am   -- Earliest any clinic or billing staff opens a dashboard --
             five hours of slack beyond the pipeline's expected finish
```

## Step 5 — Decide what happens when a clinic's file doesn't show up at all

```
- Auto Loader processes whatever files exist at trigger time; a
  missing clinic file is not an ingestion failure, it's a MISSING
  DATA condition that needs its own alert, separate from a stream
  error.
- Plan: a validation check after ingestion compares the count of
  distinct clinic_id folders touched against the expected 15, and
  posts to a shared ops channel if any clinic is missing -- so a
  late or broken export at one clinic gets noticed the same morning,
  not discovered a week later when a denial-rate number looks off.
```

## Step 6 — Confirm this plan doesn't quietly reopen the access problem

```
The nightly Auto Loader job authenticates with its own scoped
service principal -- read access to the claims-landing container
and write access to harborview.bronze only -- never a human
analyst's personal credentials and never the old shared login.
That matters here specifically because an ingestion job with
broader access than it needs would undo, in the pipeline nobody
watches at 1am, the exact governance problem the rest of this
project exists to fix on the query side.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the Auto Loader ingestion path before configuring a stream: one ADLS container with a per-clinic subfolder so one clinic's malformed export can't block the other 14, schema evolution set to addNewColumns so a legacy system adding a field doesn't halt the pipeline, and a 1am trigger that leaves five hours of buffer before the earliest dashboard open. Also planned a missing-clinic-file check, since a quiet gap is a different failure than a broken stream.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We mapped out exactly where the clinics' nightly files land and how the ingestion job will handle the inevitable differences between 15 separate legacy billing systems, plus a safety check for a clinic that doesn't send its file at all. That's the plan the actual pipeline gets built against next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned how claims data gets from each of the 15 clinics into the new platform every night, with real safety margin before anyone opens a report in the morning, and a check that catches a missing clinic's data the same day instead of a week later.

lessons.title: Provisioning Unity Catalog and the Claims Lakehouse
lessons.summary: Opening Databricks for the first time to create the harborview catalog, its bronze/silver/gold schemas, and the three Unity Catalog groups planned in Lesson 6 -- with real Terraform and SQL.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Three lessons of planning are done -- this is the first lesson where Databricks actually opens. We're provisioning the real `harborview` Unity Catalog catalog, its `bronze`, `silver`, and `gold` schemas, and the three groups designed in Lesson 6 (`compliance_team`, `clinical_quality`, `billing_analysts`) -- in Terraform, with the equivalent SQL shown alongside it so the structure is auditable either way.

Nothing lands inside these schemas yet. No `claims_raw` table, no Auto Loader stream, no row filter -- this lesson is deliberately scoped to the container and the groups, the same way a construction project pours a foundation and puts up exterior walls before anyone moves furniture in. The tables and the governance policies designed in the last three lessons get built directly on top of what's provisioned here.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine you've spent three meetings planning a new office building -- where each department sits, who gets a key to which door, what goes on each floor. This lesson is the day the actual building gets built: the foundation gets poured, the floors go up with their labels on them (bronze, silver, gold), and the front door gets three different keycards cut (one for compliance, one for clinical quality, one for billing) -- before a single desk or filing cabinet moves in. Nobody's sitting at a desk yet. The building just needs to exist first.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the first real infrastructure lesson, and the discipline worth keeping is the same one that made the planning lessons useful: provision exactly what was designed, nothing more. Terraform's `databricks_catalog` and `databricks_schema` resources create `harborview` and its three schemas as declared, version-controlled infrastructure rather than a one-off `CREATE CATALOG` someone ran by hand and nobody can diff later -- which matters directly for Harborview, since the entire reason this project exists is a prior lack of auditable, reviewable control over who could access what.

The three groups get the same treatment: `databricks_group` resources for `compliance_team`, `clinical_quality`, and `billing_analysts`, with membership managed as code rather than through a console someone might forget to document. lessons.title: Landing Claims Files With Auto Loader
lessons.summary: Standing up the Bronze layer -- Auto Loader incrementally lands nightly claims CSVs from all 15 clinics into harborview.bronze.claims_raw, append-only, with no business logic yet.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Harborview's 15 clinics each run their own legacy billing system, and each one exports a CSV of the day's claims every night into a shared cloud storage folder. Nothing about those files is standardized -- column order drifts, and a clinic occasionally adds a new field without telling anyone. This lesson builds the very first layer of the new lakehouse: a Databricks Auto Loader job that incrementally picks up every new file as it lands and writes it, untouched, into `harborview.bronze.claims_raw`. No cleaning, no validation, no business logic -- Bronze's only job is to be a faithful, append-only copy of exactly what each clinic sent, with enough metadata attached to trace any row back to the file it came from.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine 15 different mailboxes, one for each clinic, and every night each mailbox gets a new envelope stuffed with that day's claims. Instead of someone walking around every morning collecting 15 envelopes by hand, we're building a robot that checks every mailbox automatically, grabs whatever's new, and drops it straight into one big filing cabinet -- without opening the envelopes or changing anything inside them. It even writes on each piece of paper which mailbox it came from and what time the robot picked it up, so nobody ever has to guess later.
lessons.explainProfessional: This is the Bronze layer of a medallion architecture, and Auto Loader is the right tool for exactly this ingestion pattern: files of a known format (CSV) landing incrementally and unpredictably into cloud storage from systems you don't control. The two configuration choices that matter here are `cloudFiles.schemaLocation`, which persists the inferred schema between incremental runs so Auto Loader doesn't re-scan every historical file each time it checks for new ones, and `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode` set to `addNewColumns`, which means a clinic silently adding a column to its export doesn't break the pipeline -- it just shows up as a new, nullable field going forward. We write append-only with no transformation at all, because Bronze's entire value is being a reliable, replayable record of exactly what arrived; any cleaning, typing, or business logic belongs one layer up, in Silver, where it can be changed and rerun without needing to re-ingest from the clinics' original files.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm what's actually landing, and where

Harborview's 15 clinics still run on one legacy billing system per clinic. Each clinic exports a CSV of the day's claims every night and drops it into a folder in cloud object storage: `/mnt/harborview/landing/claims/`. Nobody standardized the column order across clinics, and a clinic occasionally adds a new field to its export without telling anyone. Auto Loader exists specifically for this situation -- it watches a directory for new files, infers a schema from what actually shows up, and can evolve that schema automatically instead of hard-failing the moment one clinic adds a new column.

## Step 2 — Point Auto Loader at the landing folder with `cloudFiles`

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, current_timestamp, input_file_name

raw_claims_stream = (
    spark.readStream
        .format("cloudFiles")
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")
        .option("header", "true")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/mnt/harborview/_schemas/claims_raw")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns")
        .load("/mnt/harborview/landing/claims/")
)
```

`cloudFiles.schemaLocation` is doing the real work here -- it's where Auto Loader persists the schema it infers, so every incremental run checks newly arrived files against what it's already seen instead of re-inferring from scratch. `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode` set to `addNewColumns` means a clinic adding a field doesn't break the stream; the new column appears in `claims_raw` on the next run, and any file that arrived before the column existed simply gets a null in that field.

## Step 3 — Attach traceability columns before anything touches Delta

Bronze's only job is "land it, and know where it came from." Every row gets two columns that don't exist in any clinic's CSV:

```python
bronze_claims = (
    raw_claims_stream
        .withColumn("_file_name", input_file_name())
        .withColumn("_ingested_at", current_timestamp())
)
```

`_file_name` answers "which nightly export did this row come from" months later, when a clinic's billing vendor asks why one claim looks wrong. `_ingested_at` answers "when did Databricks actually see this row," which is a different question from the claim's own date on the form -- and a question later troubleshooting in this series will eventually need answered.

## Step 4 — Write it, append-only, no business logic

```python
(
    bronze_claims.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/harborview/_checkpoints/claims_raw")
        .outputMode("append")
        .trigger(availableNow=True)
        .toTable("harborview.bronze.claims_raw")
)
```

`outputMode("append")` is non-negotiable at this layer. Bronze never updates or deletes a row that's already landed -- if a clinic's export turns out to be wrong, the fix happens downstream, in Silver, not by mutating history in Bronze. `trigger(availableNow=True)` processes every file currently sitting in the landing folder and then stops, which is the right trigger for a nightly batch job scheduled once a night, rather than a continuously running stream watching for files that only ever arrive once every 24 hours.

Notice what's deliberately absent: no type casting beyond what Auto Loader infers, no filtering of bad rows, no deduplication, no join to anything. A `claim_amount_usd` column that arrived as text stays text in Bronze. That restraint is what makes `claims_raw` safe to fully reload from scratch at any time -- it's a faithful copy of what the clinics actually sent, nothing more.

## Step 5 — Confirm the table and the checkpoint both exist

```sql
DESCRIBE DETAIL harborview.bronze.claims_raw;

SELECT _file_name, count(*)
FROM harborview.bronze.claims_raw
GROUP BY _file_name
ORDER BY _file_name DESC;
```

If every clinic's most recent file shows up with a row count that looks plausible for a day of claims, Bronze is doing its job. The checkpoint directory at `_checkpoints/claims_raw` is what lets tomorrow's run pick up exactly where tonight's left off -- Auto Loader never reprocesses a file it has already recorded as ingested.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Auto Loader's live against the claims landing folder -- cloudFiles.format is csv, schema tracked at a dedicated schemaLocation, and schemaEvolutionMode set to addNewColumns so a clinic adding a field doesn't break the stream. Writing append-only into harborview.bronze.claims_raw with _file_name and _ingested_at on every row for traceability. No business logic in this layer at all -- that's by design.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The first piece of the new claims pipeline is live: every clinic's nightly export now lands automatically into one governed table instead of sitting in 15 separate files. Nothing is being validated or cleaned yet at this stage on purpose -- that's the next lesson -- this step is just making sure nothing gets lost or missed.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The nightly claims files from all 15 clinics are now being collected automatically into one place, with a full record of exactly which file and what time each claim came from. That traceability is the foundation everything else we build -- including the governance you asked for -- depends on.

lessons.title: Building the Silver Layer With Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines
lessons.summary: The core Silver transformation -- a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline parses and dedupes Bronze claims into harborview.silver.claims_clean, with a data-quality expectation deliberately set to warn instead of drop.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Bronze gave us a faithful but untyped copy of every clinic's raw export. This lesson builds the real Silver transformation: a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline (the current name and Python API for what used to ship as Delta Live Tables) that reads harborview.bronze.claims_raw, parses and types every column, removes duplicate claims, and writes the result into harborview.silver.claims_clean. We also attach the pipeline's first real data-quality guardrail here -- checking that claim_amount_usd is positive and clinic_id isn't null -- and make a specific, deliberate choice about how strict that guardrail should be on a pipeline this new.
lessons.explainSimple: Think of Bronze as a big box of handwritten notes, some messy, some with smudges, all in different handwriting. Silver is where someone sits down, reads every note carefully, rewrites it neatly, throws out any exact duplicates, and circles anything that looks off -- like a note with no clinic written on it, or an amount that doesn't make sense. But instead of throwing the weird notes away right now, they're just circled in red and kept in the pile, because it's the first week on the job and nobody's sure yet whether 'weird' always means 'wrong.'
lessons.explainProfessional: This is the heart of the medallion architecture's Silver layer, built with Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines' Python API (`import pyspark.pipelines as dp`, `@dp.table` decorators) rather than hand-written incremental merge logic -- the pipeline engine handles the incremental bookkeeping declaratively, so the code describes the target table's contents, not the mechanics of keeping it updated. The data-quality piece is where this lesson earns its place in the series: Lakeflow's Python API supports three severities for the same expectation -- `@dp.expect` (warn: log the violation, keep the row), `@dp.expect_or_drop` (remove the violating row from the output), and `@dp.expect_or_fail` (halt the pipeline update entirely). We're attaching both expectations on `claims_clean` -- `claim_amount_usd > 0` and a non-null `clinic_id` -- at warn severity, deliberately. This is week one of a brand-new pipeline built on top of a legacy flat-file export nobody has fully audited yet, and dropping rows silently felt like too much certainty to claim this early -- a legitimate edge-case claim (a corrected $0 entry, an unusual one-off adjustment) could trip the amount check and quietly disappear from the table with no one the wiser. Warn severity keeps every row flowing while giving the pipeline's event log full visibility into exactly how often each rule actually gets violated, which is the information the team would need before ever deciding to tighten either check to drop or fail.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Set up the Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline for Silver

A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline (the modern name and API for what used to ship as Delta Live Tables) is configured as its own pipeline in Databricks, pointed at a source notebook or Python file, with a target catalog and schema of `harborview.silver`. The pipeline code uses the current, idiomatic `pyspark.pipelines` module rather than the older `dlt` module name:

```python
import pyspark.pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, trim, to_date
```

Everything from here is declarative -- you describe what `claims_clean` should contain, and the pipeline engine figures out how to keep it updated incrementally as new Bronze rows arrive, rather than you writing the incremental logic by hand.

## Step 2 — Parse, type, and dedupe the raw Bronze columns, with the expectations attached

`harborview.bronze.claims_raw` landed every column as whatever Auto Loader inferred, mostly strings. Silver's job is turning that into real, typed, trustworthy columns -- and attaching the pipeline's data-quality rules at the same time:

```python
@dp.table(
    name="claims_clean",
    comment=(
        "Silver: parsed, typed, deduplicated claims from "
        "harborview.bronze.claims_raw."
    ),
)
@dp.expect("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")
@dp.expect("valid_clinic_id", "clinic_id IS NOT NULL")
def claims_clean():
    # --- Data-quality note (read this before touching these two lines) ---
    # Both expectations above use Lakeflow's default severity -- "warn" --
    # not @dp.expect_or_drop or @dp.expect_or_fail. A warn expectation logs
    # every row that violates the rule to the pipeline's event log and
    # surfaces it in the DQ metrics, but it does NOT remove the row from
    # claims_clean and does NOT stop the pipeline update.
    #
    # This is a deliberate choice, not an oversight: this is a brand-new
    # pipeline, built from a legacy flat-file export we don't fully trust
    # yet, and silently dropping rows felt too aggressive for week one --
    # a legitimate edge-case claim (a $0 corrected claim, a clinic's
    # one-off adjustment entry) could trip the amount check and vanish
    # from the table with nobody noticing. Warn gives us visibility into
    # how often this actually happens before we decide whether "drop" or
    # "fail" is the right long-term behavior.
    return (
        dp.read_stream("harborview.bronze.claims_raw")
          .select(
              col("claim_id").cast("string"),
              trim(col("clinic_id")).cast("string").alias("clinic_id"),
              col("patient_id").cast("string"),
              col("patient_name").cast("string"),
              col("patient_ssn").cast("string"),
              to_date(col("claim_date_raw"), "yyyy-MM-dd").alias("claim_date"),
              col("claim_amount_usd").cast("decimal(12,2)"),
              col("denial_flag").cast("boolean"),
              col("_file_name"),
              col("_ingested_at"),
          )
          .dropDuplicates(["claim_id"])
    )
```

## Step 3 — Understand exactly what "warn" buys you, and what it costs

Lakeflow's Python API gives you three severities for the same expectation, and the difference between them is the entire story of this lesson:

```python
@dp.expect("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")           # warn
@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")   # drop
@dp.expect_or_fail("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")   # fail
```

`warn` keeps every row, violating or not, and just counts and logs the violations. `drop` removes a violating row from the output before it ever reaches `claims_clean`. `fail` stops the entire pipeline update the moment a violating row shows up. We chose `warn` for both expectations on `claims_clean` specifically because this pipeline just went live -- we don't yet know whether a `claim_amount_usd` of zero or less, or a missing `clinic_id`, represents a real data problem upstream or a legitimate (if unusual) claim type the legacy export produces. Warn lets rows that look bad keep flowing downstream into Gold while the metrics tell us how often the checks actually trip.

## Step 4 — Deploy and watch the event log, not just the table

```sql
SELECT expectation, passed_records, failed_records
FROM event_log(TABLE(harborview.silver.claims_clean))
WHERE event_type = 'flow_progress';
```

`failed_records` here is the number that matters this lesson. It should be small and explainable. If it's never zero and nobody's watching it, every row that failed `valid_claim_amount` or `valid_clinic_id` is still sitting in `claims_clean`, still flowing into `claims_summary_gold` and `claims_detail_gold` in the next lesson, counted as if it were clean. That gap between "the expectation exists" and "the expectation actually removes bad data" is exactly what warn severity means -- and exactly what this series comes back to later.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Silver's live: claims_clean is a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline table built with pyspark.pipelines, parsing and typing every Bronze column and deduping on claim_id. Attached two expectations -- claim_amount_usd > 0 and clinic_id IS NOT NULL -- both at warn severity using @dp.expect, not expect_or_drop or expect_or_fail. That's intentional for week one: we don't yet know if a tripped check means bad data or a legitimate edge case, so nothing's getting silently dropped until we've watched the event log for a while.
