workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Claims data is now being cleaned and deduplicated automatically every time the pipeline runs, with two quality checks watching the amount and clinic fields. We're starting those checks in a 'log it, don't remove it' mode since this is a brand-new pipeline -- we'll revisit how strict to make them once we've seen real volume.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The system is now actively checking every claim for two specific problems -- a missing or invalid amount, and a missing clinic -- and keeping a record of anything that looks off, without throwing data away while the pipeline is still new. That gives us visibility before we decide how aggressively to act on it.

lessons.title: Building the Gold Layer: Claims Summary and Claims Detail
lessons.summary: Two Gold tables built from the same clean Silver stream -- a safe clinic-level aggregate, and a patient-level detail table that is not yet access-restricted.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: harborview.silver.claims_clean is now one clean, deduplicated stream of claims. This lesson builds the two Gold tables that actually get used day to day: claims_summary_gold, a daily clinic-level rollup -- total billed amount, claim count, denial rate -- safe to hand to a broad audience because it never touches a patient's name or SSN; and claims_detail_gold, a patient-level table with one row per claim, including patient_name and patient_ssn, built for the compliance and billing teams who occasionally need that level of detail. We build both tables in this lesson, but we also say out loud that claims_detail_gold is not yet access-restricted -- that's the very next lesson's job.
lessons.explainSimple: Picture a school office that keeps two different reports. One report just says 'Mrs. Smith's class had 24 kids here today, 2 were absent' -- totally fine for anyone to see, no student names anywhere. The other report lists every single student by name with their attendance record -- useful for the school nurse or the principal, but definitely not something that should be sitting out where any visitor could read it. We're building both reports today. The first one is safe the moment it's built. The second one isn't locked up yet -- that's tomorrow's job.
lessons.explainProfessional: Gold is where the warehouse's data gets shaped for actual consumption, and this lesson is a case study in matching a table's grain to its risk profile. `claims_summary_gold` aggregates all the way down to `(clinic_id, claim_date)`, which means `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` never enter the computation at all -- there's no patient to protect in a table that was summed away from the start, so this table ships safe with zero governance work. `claims_detail_gold` keeps the claim grain and carries both identifying fields forward from Silver, which is exactly the shape compliance and billing teams need for case-level work -- and exactly the shape that needs real access control before it can be trusted with Harborview's single shared analytics login still in place. We build it here and name the gap explicitly rather than pretending it's solved, because the honest state of the project right now is: the aggregate table is done, and the detail table is correct but wide open.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Separate the two audiences Gold has to serve

`harborview.silver.claims_clean` is one clean, deduplicated stream of claims. Gold exists to shape that stream for two very different consumers: clinic administrators who want a daily rollup with no patient-level detail at all, and a compliance and billing team that occasionally needs to see an individual claim. Those are two different tables with two different risk profiles, built from the same pipeline.

## Step 2 — Build claims_summary_gold: the safe, aggregate table

```python
import pyspark.pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum, count as _count, col

@dp.table(
    name="claims_summary_gold",
    comment=(
        "Gold: daily, clinic-level aggregate -- total billed amount, "
        "claim count, and denial rate. Contains no patient-identifying data."
    ),
)
def claims_summary_gold():
    claims = dp.read("claims_clean")
    return (
        claims.groupBy("clinic_id", "claim_date")
              .agg(
                  _sum("claim_amount_usd").alias("total_billed_usd"),
                  _count("claim_id").alias("claim_count"),
                  (
                      _sum(col("denial_flag").cast("int"))
                      / _count("claim_id")
                  ).alias("denial_rate"),
              )
    )
```

Nothing in `claims_summary_gold` identifies a patient -- it's grouped all the way down to `clinic_id` and `claim_date`, so `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` never even enter the aggregation. That makes this table safe to hand to a much wider audience than the detail table in the next step, and it's the table this series' dashboards will actually point at for clinic-level reporting.

## Step 3 — Build claims_detail_gold: the table that still needs a lock on the door

```python
@dp.table(
    name="claims_detail_gold",
    comment=(
        "Gold: one row per claim, patient-level detail including "
        "patient_name and patient_ssn. NOT access-restricted at this "
        "point in the build -- anyone with SELECT on this table can see "
        "every clinic's patients today. Row-level security is added in "
        "Lessons 12-13."
    ),
)
def claims_detail_gold():
    return (
        dp.read("claims_clean")
          .select(
              "claim_id",
              "clinic_id",
              "patient_id",
              "patient_name",
              "patient_ssn",
              "claim_date",
              "claim_amount_usd",
              "denial_flag",
          )
    )
```

Read that table comment carefully, because it's describing the exact state Harborview started this whole project to fix: `claims_detail_gold` carries `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` for every clinic, and as of this lesson, there is still no governance on it at all. Anyone granted `SELECT` on `harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold` -- which, right now, is still the one shared analytics login with full access -- sees every patient at every clinic, not just the ones they should.

## Step 4 — Confirm both tables build correctly before moving on

```sql
SELECT clinic_id, claim_date, total_billed_usd, claim_count, denial_rate
FROM harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
ORDER BY claim_date DESC
LIMIT 20;

SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT clinic_id)
FROM harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold;
```

The summary table should show one row per clinic per day with a denial rate between 0 and 1. The detail table's row count should roughly match `claims_clean`'s row count -- this is a pass-through select, not an aggregation, so no row should disappear or multiply between Silver and this Gold table.

## Step 5 — Name the gap explicitly, out loud, before the next lesson

`claims_summary_gold` ships clean. `claims_detail_gold` does not. Say that plainly to whoever's tracking this build: the detail table exists, it's correct, and it is currently wide open to anyone with catalog access -- which is exactly the problem described in Harborview's original ask, just rebuilt one layer higher in the new platform instead of solved. That gap is the entire subject of the next lesson.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built both Gold tables off claims_clean: claims_summary_gold groups to clinic_id/claim_date for total billed, claim count, and denial rate -- no patient fields anywhere in it. claims_detail_gold is a pass-through at claim grain, still carrying patient_name and patient_ssn. Flagging clearly: claims_detail_gold has zero access restriction right now -- same exposure problem as the old shared login, just one layer up. That's lesson 12's scope, not closed yet.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have the clinic-level summary report ready to use safely today, and the detailed, patient-level table built and verified -- but not yet locked down. I want to be upfront that the detail table isn't safe to open up to broader access until the next step in the build closes that gap.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built the clinic-level reporting you'll use for day-to-day numbers, and it's safe to share broadly right now -- no patient names or SSNs anywhere in it. The detailed, patient-level table is also built, but it isn't locked down yet -- that's the very next thing we're doing, and until then, access to it should stay limited to the same small group that has it today.

lessons.title: Applying Row-Level Security With Unity Catalog Row Filters
lessons.summary: Closing the governance gap on claims_detail_gold with a real Unity Catalog row filter function, restricting non-compliance users to only their assigned clinic's rows.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: This lesson closes the gap named at the end of the last one. claims_detail_gold carries patient_name and patient_ssn for every clinic, and right now anyone with SELECT on it sees every patient at every clinic -- the exact problem Harborview hired us to fix, just rebuilt one layer higher in the new platform. We fix it with real Unity Catalog row-level security: a clinic-assignment lookup table, a SQL row filter function that checks a user's group membership and their assigned clinics, and one ALTER TABLE statement that attaches the filter directly to claims_detail_gold's metadata in the catalog.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine a filing cabinet where every drawer has every patient's folder mixed together, and anyone with a key to the cabinet can open any drawer. What we're building is like replacing that one master key with ID badges -- when you swipe your badge, the cabinet only shows you the drawers for your own clinic, automatically, every single time, no matter which door you use to get in. A special badge for the compliance team still opens every drawer, because that's genuinely part of their job -- but a regular clinic badge only ever opens that clinic's drawer.
lessons.explainProfessional: Unity Catalog row filters are the mechanism that finally makes this governance model enforceable rather than aspirational: the filter is a SQL function returning a boolean per row, attached to the table itself via `ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER`, and evaluated by the engine on every single query against that table -- a dashboard, an ad hoc notebook, a BI tool -- with no way for a querying user to bypass it by changing how they ask. The function itself encodes the actual access policy as a short-circuit OR: `is_account_group_member('compliance_team')` grants unrestricted visibility to the one group that legitimately needs cross-clinic access, and everyone else falls through to an EXISTS check against a `clinic_access_lookup` table keyed on `current_user()` and `clinic_id`. That lookup table is the single source of truth for who sees what -- not a hardcoded list inside the function, not a per-dashboard filter someone has to remember to add. Verifying this lesson means more than confirming the SQL compiles: it means actually querying the table as a real non-compliance user and confirming the result set is restricted, and querying again as a compliance-group member and confirming it isn't.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Build the clinic-assignment lookup table

Row-level security needs a source of truth for "which users are allowed to see which clinic's rows." Harborview doesn't have this mapped anywhere yet, so we build it as a real governed table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS harborview.gold.clinic_access_lookup (
  user_email STRING,
  clinic_id  STRING
)
USING DELTA;

INSERT INTO harborview.gold.clinic_access_lookup VALUES
  ('admin.northside@harborview.org', 'CLINIC_01'),
  ('admin.northside@harborview.org', 'CLINIC_02'),
  ('admin.eastgate@harborview.org',  'CLINIC_07');
```

Each row grants one user visibility into one clinic. A user assigned to several clinics just gets several rows. This table is the only place that mapping lives -- not hardcoded into a view, not maintained by hand in a spreadsheet.

## Step 2 — Write the row filter function

Unity Catalog row filters are backed by a SQL function that returns a boolean for each row, evaluated against the querying user's identity at query time:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION harborview.gold.clinic_row_filter(clinic_id STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN
  is_account_group_member('compliance_team')
  OR EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM harborview.gold.clinic_access_lookup AS a
    WHERE a.user_email = current_user()
      AND a.clinic_id  = clinic_row_filter.clinic_id
  );
```

Two conditions, joined with `OR`: `is_account_group_member('compliance_team')` grants full, unrestricted visibility to anyone in that Unity Catalog account group -- compliance and billing staff who legitimately need to see across clinics. Everyone else falls through to the `EXISTS` subquery, which checks `clinic_access_lookup` for a row matching both `current_user()` and the specific `clinic_id` of the row being evaluated. No match, no row.

## Step 3 — Apply the filter to claims_detail_gold

```sql
ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
SET ROW FILTER harborview.gold.clinic_row_filter ON (clinic_id);
```

This single statement is what actually closes the gap from the last lesson. From this point on, every query against `claims_detail_gold` -- a `SELECT *`, a BI dashboard, an ad hoc notebook query -- has this filter applied automatically by Unity Catalog, before a single row of patient data leaves the table. Nobody querying the table has to remember to add a `WHERE clinic_id = ...` clause themselves, and nobody can bypass it by querying a different way, because the filter is attached to the table's metadata in the catalog, not to any one query or dashboard.

## Step 4 — Verify it actually restricts, not just that it runs

```sql
-- as a clinic-assigned, non-compliance user
SELECT DISTINCT clinic_id FROM harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold;
-- should return only the clinic(s) that user has rows for in
-- clinic_access_lookup

-- as a member of the compliance_team account group
SELECT DISTINCT clinic_id FROM harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold;
-- should return all 15 clinics
```

A row filter that compiles but doesn't actually change query results is worse than no filter at all, because it looks solved on a diagram and isn't. Test both sides of the `OR` explicitly, with real accounts in each group, before calling this done.

## Step 5 — Confirm claims_summary_gold doesn't need this at all

`claims_summary_gold` has no `patient_name`, no `patient_ssn`, and no row below the clinic-day grain -- there's no patient to protect in a table that was aggregated away from the start. Applying a row filter there would be governance theater, not governance. The lesson worth carrying forward: row-level security belongs on the table that actually carries the sensitive grain, and a well-designed aggregate table can sometimes avoid needing it entirely.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Closed the governance gap on claims_detail_gold. Built clinic_access_lookup as the source of truth for user-to-clinic mapping, wrote clinic_row_filter as a SQL function -- is_account_group_member('compliance_team') OR an EXISTS check against the lookup keyed on current_user() and clinic_id -- and attached it with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER. Verified both sides: a clinic-assigned user only sees their own clinic's rows, a compliance_team member sees all 15. claims_summary_gold doesn't need this -- it's aggregated past the point of having a patient to protect.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The patient-level claims table is now actually restricted by clinic, enforced automatically by the platform itself rather than relying on anyone remembering to filter a report correctly. We tested this with real accounts on both sides -- a regular clinic user and a compliance team member -- and confirmed each one sees exactly what they should.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The exact problem that started this project -- one shared login with full access to every patient's name and SSN across all 15 clinics -- is now fixed at the data layer itself, not just in a dashboard setting someone could change. Clinic staff only ever see their own clinic's patients; your compliance team retains the full view it legitimately needs. This is real governance, built into the platform, not a policy on paper.

lessons.title: Applying Column Masking and Data Classification Tags
lessons.summary: Writing real Unity Catalog column masks for patient_name and patient_ssn on claims_detail_gold, plus PHI classification tags that make the masked columns discoverable in an audit.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 12 built Unity Catalog row filters so a clinic-floor analyst only ever sees their own clinic's rows in `harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold`. That controls *which rows* someone can see — it says nothing about what two of the columns inside a visible row actually contain. This lesson adds the other half: a SQL masking function that redacts `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` for anyone outside the `compliance_team` account-console group, applied with `ALTER TABLE ... SET MASK`, plus Unity Catalog data classification tags on both columns so the fact that they carry PHI is discoverable in a schema browse or an audit query, not just known to whoever wrote the `ALTER TABLE` statement.

Row filters and column masks are independent mechanisms that compose automatically. By the end of this lesson, a non-compliance analyst at Clinic 4 still sees only Clinic 4's claims (Lesson 12), and on every one of those rows, `patient_name` and `patient_ssn` read `REDACTED` (this lesson) — two separate, separately-granted controls, stacked on the same table, neither one aware of the other.
lessons.explainSimple:
Row filters, from last lesson, are like being handed only the folders with your own name on them. Masking is different: even once you're holding a real folder, a masking rule can black out two specific lines on the page inside it — like someone's social security number — unless you're on the short list of people allowed to read that line.

So two people can both be holding the exact same folder. One of them, on the compliance list, sees the real name and the real number. Everyone else sees the word REDACTED where that information used to be, even though they're looking at the same page.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Unity Catalog's column mask is a SQL function, registered once in the catalog and attached to a column with `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK`, evaluated per row at query time against the querying principal's identity — the same `is_account_group_member()` primitive the Lesson 12 row filters already rely on. The two mechanisms are deliberately orthogonal: a row filter decides whether a row is visible at all; a mask decides what a visible row's column contains. Neither one needs to know the other exists, which is exactly what makes them composable instead of one large, harder-to-audit combined policy that would need updating in two places every time either rule changed.

The second half of this lesson — data classification tags — is a governance concern distinct from access control. `SET TAGS ('pii_category' = 'phi')` doesn't restrict anything by itself; it makes the column's sensitivity queryable through `system.information_schema.column_tags`, which is what turns "someone remembers patient_ssn is sensitive" into an auditable fact a compliance review can actually run a query against. A masked column with no tag still works correctly for access control, but it's invisible to anyone doing a PHI inventory who didn't already know to look at that specific table — the tag is what makes the masking decision itself discoverable, not just effective.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Decide what has to be masked, and for whom, before writing SQL

`harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold` carries two columns Harborview's compliance officer flagged during the Lesson 12 row-filter work: `patient_name` and `patient_ssn`. The rule is simple to state: anyone in the `compliance_team` account-console group sees the real value; everyone else — including a clinic-floor analyst with a legitimate row-filter grant to their own clinic's claims — sees a redacted placeholder, never the real name or SSN.

## Step 2 — Write the masking function for patient_ssn

A column mask is a SQL function returning the same type as the column it masks, evaluated per row:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION harborview.gold.mask_patient_ssn(ssn STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN is_account_group_member('compliance_team') THEN ssn
  ELSE 'REDACTED'
END;
```

`is_account_group_member()` checks the querying user's group membership at execution time — the same mechanism Lesson 12's row filters already use, so nothing new has to be provisioned to reuse it here.

## Step 3 — Write the masking function for patient_name, and apply both

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION harborview.gold.mask_patient_name(name STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN is_account_group_member('compliance_team') THEN name
  ELSE 'REDACTED'
END;

ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
ALTER COLUMN patient_ssn
SET MASK harborview.gold.mask_patient_ssn;

ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
ALTER COLUMN patient_name
SET MASK harborview.gold.mask_patient_name;
```

Each `ALTER COLUMN ... SET MASK` attaches a function to exactly one column. Nothing about the table's storage changes, and no existing query against `claims_detail_gold` needs to change — the mask evaluates transparently the next time anyone runs a `SELECT`.

## Step 4 — Add data classification tags, separately from the mask itself

A mask controls access. A tag makes the fact that a column needs one discoverable to someone who isn't the person who wrote it — a future engineer, an auditor, or Harborview's own quarterly PHI inventory:

```sql
ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
ALTER COLUMN patient_ssn SET TAGS ('pii_category' = 'phi');

ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
ALTER COLUMN patient_name SET TAGS ('pii_category' = 'phi');
```

## Step 5 — Confirm the tags are actually queryable, not just set

```sql
SELECT table_name, column_name, tag_name, tag_value
FROM system.information_schema.column_tags
WHERE table_catalog = 'harborview'
  AND table_name = 'claims_detail_gold';
```

This is the query Harborview's compliance team will actually run every quarter — the tag only earns its keep if it shows up here, in one place, instead of living only in whoever's memory wrote the original `ALTER TABLE` statement.

## Step 6 — Test the mask as two different users, not just as yourself

Masking logic that only ever gets tested by the person who wrote it — who is almost always already in `compliance_team` — proves nothing. Ask a teammate who is not in that group to run:

```sql
SELECT claim_id, clinic_id, patient_name, patient_ssn
FROM harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
LIMIT 5;
```

From `compliance_team`, both columns return real values. From any other account, both return `REDACTED`.

## Step 7 — Confirm row filters and masks compose, they don't conflict

Run the same query as a Clinic 4 analyst who is not in `compliance_team`: they see only Clinic 4's claims (the Lesson 12 row filter), and `patient_name`/`patient_ssn` read `REDACTED` on every one of those rows (this lesson's masks). Neither mechanism overrides the other — Unity Catalog evaluates both independently, every time, which is exactly why they were built as two separate grants instead of one combined rule that would need updating twice every time either policy changed.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Added Unity Catalog column masks on patient_name and patient_ssn in claims_detail_gold, gated on compliance_team membership through the same is_account_group_member() primitive Lesson 12's row filters already use, plus pii_category=phi classification tags on both columns so they're discoverable in system.information_schema.column_tags for an audit. Verified by testing as both a compliance_team member and a non-member, and confirmed masks and row filters compose correctly on the same table.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Patient names and SSNs in the claims detail table are now automatically hidden from anyone outside the compliance team, on top of the clinic-based access control we already built. Both columns are also now formally tagged as protected health information, so a compliance audit can find them by running one query instead of relying on someone remembering where they are.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Patient names and social security numbers in our claims data are now hidden from everyone except the compliance team, automatically, no matter which clinic's data someone is authorized to see. We've also formally labeled those fields as protected health information inside the system, so our next compliance audit can verify that on its own.

lessons.title: Orchestrating the Pipeline With Databricks Workflows
lessons.summary: Wiring a three-task Databricks Workflows job — Bronze ingestion, the Silver Lakeflow pipeline, Gold refresh — into one nightly, dependency-ordered schedule with failure alerting.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything built so far — the Lesson 9 Auto Loader ingestion into `claims_raw`, the Lesson 10 Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that produces `claims_clean`, and the Lesson 11 aggregation into `claims_summary_gold` and `claims_detail_gold` — only runs when someone manually kicks each step off, in the right order, by hand. This lesson wires all three into a single Databricks Workflows job, `harborview_claims_nightly`: a Bronze ingestion task, a Silver pipeline-update task, and a Gold refresh task, each one gated on the task before it finishing successfully, scheduled to run on its own every night, with a failure alert wired to all three tasks, not just the last one.

This is the piece that turns a pipeline that works when you run it into a pipeline that reliably runs itself. Harborview's clinics, Finance, and the compliance reviews built in Lessons 12 and 13 only matter if the data underneath them is actually fresh every morning without anyone opening a notebook.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture three relay runners: one fetches the baton (loads the raw claims), the second one carries it most of the way (cleans it up), and the third one carries it across the finish line (adds it all up into the reports). Databricks Workflows is the race official standing at the side with a clipboard, making sure runner two never starts before runner one has actually finished, and runner three never starts before runner two has — and blowing a whistle loudly the moment any one of them trips, instead of just quietly writing it down.

Every single night, without anyone pressing a button, this relay runs itself, in the same order, at the same time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is pipeline orchestration, and the design decision that matters most is making the dependency chain explicit rather than hoped-for. The job has three tasks: `bronze_ingest_claims_raw` (a notebook task running the Lesson 9 Auto Loader ingestion), `silver_pipeline_update` (a `pipeline_task` that triggers an update of the `claims_clean` Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline from Lesson 10), and `gold_refresh` (a notebook task recomputing `claims_summary_gold` and `claims_detail_gold` from Lesson 11) — wired with `depends_on` so each task only starts once the one before it reports success.

The schedule, a 2 AM cron expression, runs after Harborview's 15 clinics finish submitting the day's claims batches and after the clinics' own billing export has already run — which matters directly in Lesson 15, since that export is the independent number Finance ends up comparing the pipeline's output against. `max_concurrent_runs: 1` prevents a slow night's run from ever overlapping with the next one, the same role Airflow's `max_active_runs` plays in other tracks' nightly DAGs. Failure alerting is wired to the job as a whole rather than to `gold_refresh` alone, so a Bronze-layer failure reaches a human immediately instead of letting the job silently skip straight to reporting on yesterday's stale Gold tables.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built the harborview_claims_nightly Workflows job: three tasks — Auto Loader ingestion, the claims_clean Lakeflow pipeline update, and the Gold refresh notebook — chained with depends_on so each only starts after the previous one succeeds. Scheduled for 2am, after clinic submissions and the billing export both close, with max_concurrent_runs set to 1 and a failure alert wired to all three tasks, then proved the dependency chain actually blocks a bad run by breaking Bronze on purpose and confirming Silver and Gold skipped instead of running on stale data.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The whole nightly pipeline now runs itself, in the right order, with nobody needing to kick off each step by hand. If any part of it fails — loading the raw claims, cleaning them, or building the reports — the team is alerted immediately instead of finding out because a number looks wrong the next morning.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The claims pipeline now runs automatically every night on a fixed schedule, timed to come after the clinics finish submitting the day's claims. If anything goes wrong at any step, the team is alerted right away rather than finding out later from a report that looks off.

lessons.title: Finance Flags a Claims Total That Doesn't Reconcile
lessons.summary: Finance says the August claims-dollar total in claims_summary_gold doesn't match the clinics' own billing export. Tracing the number layer by layer from Bronze through Gold finds exactly where, and by how much, it first goes wrong.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The governance work in Lessons 12 and 13, and the nightly orchestration in Lesson 14, only matter if the numbers underneath them are actually correct. Dana Okafor, Harborview's VP of Finance, flags in the Monday pipeline review that the August dollar total in `claims_summary_gold` doesn't match the clinics' own billing-system export for the same month. The easy, wrong move is to start debugging Gold's aggregation SQL, since that's the number Finance is looking at. This lesson resists that instinct and instead traces the number layer by layer — `claims_raw`, then `claims_clean`, then `claims_summary_gold` — for the identical date range, narrowing down exactly where the two numbers first diverge before writing a single line of fix.

The investigation finds that Bronze and Finance's own export agree exactly, that Gold is faithfully summing whatever Silver hands it, and that the real discrepancy already exists inside `claims_clean` itself — a specific, small set of claims with negative dollar amounts that should never have been allowed through.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a cash register receipt that's supposed to match what's actually in the till at the end of the day, and it doesn't — it's short by a specific amount. You wouldn't start by assuming the whole till is broken. You'd count the cash drawer first, then check it against the register tape, then check the register tape against the final total on the receipt, one step at a time, until you find the exact point where the numbers stop agreeing.

That's exactly what happens here. The claims total that Finance says looks wrong gets checked against the step before it, and the step before that, until the search lands on a small handful of claims that were never supposed to be allowed to have a negative dollar amount in the first place.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is layer-by-layer data validation, and the discipline that matters is resisting the pull to debug the layer the complaint is actually about before ruling out every layer upstream of it. Finance's number and `claims_summary_gold`'s number disagree by $37,120, with Gold reporting *less* than the clinics' own export — a shortfall, not an overcount, which from the very first comparison already rules out a double-counting join and points toward something being excluded or subtracted that shouldn't be.

Pulling the identical August date range from `claims_raw` shows it matches the clinics' billing export exactly — ingestion is clean. Pulling the same range from `claims_clean` shows the same row count as Bronze, so nothing was dropped, but the dollar sum is already $37,120 short — the exact same gap Finance flagged, proving the discrepancy originates inside Silver, not Gold. Checking `claims_summary_gold` against `claims_clean` confirms Gold's own `SUM()` is correct on the data it was handed; the search for root cause ends entirely at the Gold layer. A same-row-count, lower-sum signature is the specific shape of a negative value hiding somewhere in the data, not a missing or duplicated row — and spot-checking for exactly that surfaces fourteen claims, all from one clinic, all negative, summing to precisely the missing amount.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Get Finance's exact number and the exact point of comparison

Dana Okafor, Harborview's VP of Finance, flags it directly: the August `claims_summary_gold` dollar total doesn't match the clinics' own billing-system export for the same month. Get both numbers exactly, not paraphrased.

```sql
-- claims_summary_gold, August 2026, all clinics
SELECT SUM(total_billed_usd)
FROM harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
WHERE claim_date BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31';
-- $2,114,860

-- Clinics' own billing-system export for the same month: $2,151,980
```

A $37,120 shortfall — `claims_summary_gold` reports less than the clinics say they billed. That direction matters: a shortfall rules out a double-counting join from the start and points toward something being excluded or subtracted that shouldn't be.

## Step 2 — Don't assume Gold is broken — check every layer, in order

The pipeline has three layers: `claims_raw`, `claims_clean`, `claims_summary_gold`. The discrepancy could originate in any of them. Pull the same date range from each and compare before touching any code.

## Step 3 — Pull the Bronze sample first

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(CAST(claim_amount_usd AS DECIMAL(12,2)))
FROM harborview.bronze.claims_raw
WHERE claim_date BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31';
-- 18,442 rows, SUM = $2,151,980
```

`claims_raw`'s sum matches the clinics' billing export exactly. Whatever is wrong, it isn't happening at ingestion.

## Step 4 — Compare Silver against Bronze for the same range

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(claim_amount_usd)
FROM harborview.silver.claims_clean
WHERE claim_date BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31';
-- 18,442 rows, SUM = $2,114,860
```

Same row count as Bronze — nothing got dropped on the way through `claims_clean` — but the sum is already $37,120 short, the exact gap Finance flagged. The discrepancy is proven to originate in Silver, not in Gold's aggregation.

## Step 5 — Confirm Gold is innocent before moving on

```sql
SELECT SUM(total_billed_usd)
FROM harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
WHERE claim_date BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31';
-- $2,114,860
```

Matches `claims_clean`'s sum exactly. Gold's `SUM()` is doing its job correctly on the data it was given — the search narrows entirely to why Silver's total is lower than Bronze's when both have the same row count.

## Step 6 — Same row count, lower sum — look for the shape of the gap

An identical row count with a lower sum means the dollar amounts themselves changed somewhere between Bronze and Silver. Spot-check for the one shape of row that can lower a sum without changing a row count: a negative value.

```sql
SELECT claim_id, clinic_id, claim_amount_usd, claim_date
FROM harborview.silver.claims_clean
WHERE claim_date BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31'
  AND claim_amount_usd < 0
ORDER BY claim_amount_usd;
-- 14 rows, all clinic_id = 'CLINIC-11', totaling -$37,120
```

Fourteen claims, every one from Clinic 11, every one negative, summing to exactly the missing $37,120.

## Step 7 — Confirm the same rows in Bronze, to rule out a Silver-side corruption

```sql
SELECT claim_id, claim_amount_usd
FROM harborview.bronze.claims_raw
WHERE claim_id IN (<the 14 claim_ids from Step 6>);
-- same 14 rows, same negative amounts, already negative in Bronze
```

The negative amounts aren't a transformation bug introduced inside `claims_clean` — they arrived negative, straight out of Clinic 11's practice-management export, and `claims_clean` let every one of them through unchanged.

## Step 8 — Name exactly what's proven, and what isn't yet

```text
PROVEN: claims_raw and the clinics' billing export agree exactly -- ingestion is clean.
PROVEN: the $37,120 gap first appears between claims_raw and claims_clean, with
        row counts identical on both sides -- no rows were dropped or duplicated.
PROVEN: 14 negative-amount claims, all from Clinic 11, already negative in
        Bronze, sum to exactly the missing $37,120.
NOT YET PROVEN: why claims_clean's own data-quality rules didn't stop 14 claims
        with claim_amount_usd <= 0 from reaching Silver in the first place.
```

A claim amount should never be able to be negative — that's precisely the kind of row `claims_clean`'s Lesson 10 expectations were written to catch. Lesson 16 opens that pipeline's actual code to find out why they didn't.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Traced Finance's reconciliation complaint layer by layer: claims_raw matches the clinics' billing export exactly, claims_clean has the same row count as Bronze but a $37,120 lower sum, and claims_summary_gold faithfully sums whatever claims_clean hands it. Isolated the gap to 14 negative-amount claims from Clinic 11 that were already negative in Bronze and passed straight through Silver unchanged. Haven't opened claims_clean's expectation code yet, but know exactly what to look for.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We confirmed the claims total Finance flagged really doesn't reconcile, and traced exactly where the number goes wrong — it's not the raw data and it's not the report logic, it's a small batch of claims from one clinic with an impossible negative dollar amount that made it into the clean data. We know precisely which claims and which clinic, and we're ready to fix the control that should have caught this.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We confirmed Finance's concern about this month's claims total was correct, and traced it to a small number of claims from one clinic that had an impossible negative dollar value. We know exactly which claims are responsible and where the gap in our process is, and we're fixing it next so this can't recur.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing a Data-Quality Expectation That Only Warned Instead of Dropping
lessons.summary: Reading claims_clean's real Lakeflow expectation code to find out why a rule checking claim_amount_usd > 0 let 14 negative claims through, fixing the severity, backfilling the already-landed bad rows, and adding monitoring so a warn-severity spike gets watched going forward.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved the $37,120 reconciliation gap comes from 14 negative-amount claims that reached `claims_clean` and stayed there. This lesson opens that pipeline's actual code and finds the exact reason: a data-quality expectation checking `claim_amount_usd > 0` and non-null `clinic_id` was already in place — it was never missing — but it was configured at Lakeflow's warn severity, which logs a violation and keeps the row, instead of drop or fail severity, which would have kept it out.

The fix isn't rewriting the business rule; the condition was already correct. It's changing the enforcement level for the two expectations that feed a financial total, reprocessing `claims_clean` through the corrected rule to retroactively remove the 14 bad rows, recomputing `claims_summary_gold`, and adding a monitor on the warn-severity violation count so a future spike reaches a person within the hour instead of surfacing three weeks later as a number Finance can't reconcile.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a smoke detector that's working perfectly — it really does sound an alarm every time it senses smoke — except someone wired it to a notepad instead of a loud alarm, so every time it detects smoke, it just quietly writes "smoke detected" on a piece of paper that nobody is reading. The detector was never broken. Its wiring just wasn't set up to actually stop anything.

That's exactly what happened here. The rule checking for impossible negative claim amounts was working exactly as built — it caught every single one — but it was wired to just write down the problem instead of stopping the bad claims from going through. The fix is rewiring it to actually block those rows, cleaning up the ones that already got through, and this time, actually reading the notepad.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The root cause is a severity-level choice, not a missing or incorrect rule. `claims_clean`'s Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline already declares `@dp.expect("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")` and `@dp.expect("valid_clinic_id", "clinic_id IS NOT NULL")` — both rules check exactly the right condition. A bare `@dp.expect(...)`, with no `_or_drop` or `_or_fail` suffix, defaults to warn severity: Lakeflow evaluates the condition against every row, increments a `failed_records` counter in the pipeline's event log, and keeps the row regardless of the result. The expectation was never silent about the problem — the pipeline's own event log already had 14 failed records logged against `valid_claim_amount` on the exact run that landed Clinic 11's claims — it simply wasn't configured to act on what it found, and nothing was watching that counter.

Warn wasn't a careless default when this was built; it's defensible for a rule where a legitimate edge case can look like a violation without being one — a clinic re-submitting a claim at a corrected, unusually low amount, for instance. That reasoning stops applying the moment a rule's violation changes a number Finance reports externally, which `valid_claim_amount` and `valid_clinic_id` both do. The fix changes only the severity, to `expect_or_drop`, for those two rules — every other `expect` rule in the pipeline stays at warn, deliberately, because most of them aren't gating a financial total. Because `claims_clean` is a managed streaming table inside a declarative pipeline, the correct way to remove the already-landed bad rows isn't a manual `DELETE` — it's a full refresh, which replays the immutable `claims_raw` log through the corrected expectations and drops the 14 rows retroactively, exactly as if `expect_or_drop` had been in place from the start.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Read claims_clean's actual pipeline code, not a guess at it

```python
import pyspark.pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, trim

@dp.table(name="claims_clean")
@dp.expect("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")
@dp.expect("valid_clinic_id", "clinic_id IS NOT NULL")
def claims_clean():
    return (dp.read_stream("harborview.bronze.claims_raw")
        .select(col("claim_id").cast("string"),
                trim(col("clinic_id")).alias("clinic_id"),
                col("claim_amount_usd").cast("decimal(12,2)"))
        .dropDuplicates(["claim_id"]))
```

This is the exact definition from Lesson 10, unchanged — `claim_amount_usd > 0` is already being checked, exactly as it should be, along with a non-null `clinic_id`. (The full definition also passes through `claim_date`, `patient_id`, `patient_name`, `patient_ssn`, and `denial_flag` unchanged — `claims_detail_gold` in Lesson 11 selects all of them straight out of `claims_clean` — trimmed here to the three columns the two expectations actually touch.) The bare `@dp.expect(...)` decorator — with no `_or_drop` or `_or_fail` suffix — defaults to **warn** severity: Lakeflow checks every row against the rule, counts every violation, and keeps every row regardless of the result. The expectation was never missing or wrong; it simply wasn't configured to do anything about a failure.

## Step 2 — Confirm that with the pipeline's own numbers, not an assumption

```sql
SELECT
  exp.name,
  exp.passed_records,
  exp.failed_records
FROM event_log(TABLE(harborview.silver.claims_clean)),
     LATERAL VIEW explode(
       details:flow_progress:data_quality:expectations) t AS exp
WHERE event_type = 'flow_progress'
  AND exp.name = 'valid_claim_amount'
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 1;

-- name: valid_claim_amount | passed_records: 18,428 | failed_records: 14
```

The pipeline's own event log already knew. Fourteen rows failed `valid_claim_amount` on the exact run that landed Clinic 11's claims, and all fourteen were kept anyway — the metric was always there to find, logged and queryable, just never watched by anyone or wired to an alert.

## Step 3 — Give warn its due before changing anything

Warn wasn't a careless default when this pipeline was built — it was a deliberate call. A legitimate correction claim can look unusual without being wrong, and dropping every row that fails any expectation risks silently losing a real claim nobody meant to discard. That reasoning still holds for plenty of other rules in this pipeline. It stops holding specifically for a rule whose violation changes a number Finance reports — and `valid_claim_amount` is exactly that rule.

## Step 4 — Make the fix: change severity, not the rule itself

```python
import pyspark.pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, trim

@dp.table(name="claims_clean")
@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_claim_amount", "claim_amount_usd > 0")
@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_clinic_id", "clinic_id IS NOT NULL")
def claims_clean():
    return (dp.read_stream("harborview.bronze.claims_raw")
        .select(col("claim_id").cast("string"),
                trim(col("clinic_id")).alias("clinic_id"),
                col("claim_amount_usd").cast("decimal(12,2)"))
        .dropDuplicates(["claim_id"]))
```

The condition — `claim_amount_usd > 0` — never changes; it was already correct. Only the enforcement level changes, from `expect` to `expect_or_drop`, for the two rules that feed a financial total: a negative or unidentified-clinic claim no longer reaches `claims_clean` at all.

## Step 5 — Backfill: reprocess, don't hand-edit

`claims_clean` is a managed streaming table inside a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline — the correct way to remove the 14 already-landed bad rows is a full refresh, not a manual `DELETE`. A full refresh replays every historical micro-batch out of the immutable `claims_raw` log through the now-corrected expectations, dropping the 14 Clinic 11 rows retroactively:

```text
Pipelines UI -> harborview_claims_clean_pipeline -> claims_clean -> Full refresh
```

Then re-run the `gold_refresh` task from Lesson 14's job so `claims_summary_gold` recomputes from the now-clean Silver layer.

## Step 6 — Verify against the Lesson 15 numbers

```sql
SELECT SUM(total_billed_usd)
FROM harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
WHERE claim_date BETWEEN '2026-08-01' AND '2026-08-31';
-- $2,151,980
```

Matches the clinics' billing export exactly — the $37,120 gap is closed, and `claims_clean` and `claims_summary_gold` both now agree with Bronze and with Finance.

## Step 7 — Watch the warn count going forward, not just this once

`valid_claim_amount` and `valid_clinic_id` are fixed. Every other `expect` rule in the pipeline stays at warn, deliberately — the fix isn't "stop using warn," it's "watch the warn count instead of only logging it." Add a Databricks SQL alert on the same event-log query from Step 2, scheduled hourly, that fires the moment any expectation's `failed_records` is greater than zero on a run. A warn-severity violation now reaches a human within the hour instead of surfacing weeks later as a number Finance can't reconcile.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Root cause: claims_clean's valid_claim_amount and valid_clinic_id expectations were correctly checking claim_amount_usd > 0 and non-null clinic_id, but both were at Lakeflow's default warn severity, which logs a violation and keeps the row. Confirmed via the pipeline's event log that 14 rows failed valid_claim_amount and were kept anyway. Fixed by switching both to expect_or_drop, full-refreshed claims_clean to retroactively remove the 14 bad rows, recomputed claims_summary_gold (now matches the billing export exactly), and added an hourly SQL alert on failed_records so a warn-severity spike reaches someone going forward instead of only being logged.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found and fixed the real cause of the claims-total mismatch: a data-quality check was correctly catching 14 bad claims every time, but was only set to log the problem instead of blocking it. It's fixed, the affected rows have been removed and the report recalculated to match the clinics' own records exactly, and we've added an alert so a similar issue gets caught within the hour instead of showing up in next month's numbers.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found and corrected the cause of this month's claims total being off: a safeguard was working and had already flagged the problem rows, but wasn't configured to stop them from counting. That's fixed, the number now matches the clinics' own billing records exactly, and we've added an automatic alert so a similar issue is caught immediately going forward instead of surfacing in a report later.

lessons.title: Connecting Power BI to Claims Summary Gold, Governed End to End
lessons.summary: Wiring Power BI to claims_summary_gold only — never claims_detail_gold — so the dashboard itself can't become a side door around the row filters and column masks built earlier in this series.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the gold layer built, the row filters and column masks in place on `claims_detail_gold`, and the negative-claims expectation bug fixed, backfilled, and monitored, Harborview's first real business consumption point is a Power BI report for clinical leadership and the Finance team: billed claim totals and denial rates by clinic, rolled up to a monthly trend, across all 15 clinics.

This video connects Power BI to exactly one table — `harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold` — and treats that choice as load-bearing, not incidental. The report never queries `claims_detail_gold`. That's not a style preference; it's the thing that keeps this dashboard from quietly becoming a way around the clinic-based row filters and the patient-name/SSN masks built in earlier lessons, since a report that could reach the row-level table could, in principle, reconstruct exactly what those controls were built to prevent.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a hospital has a giant locked filing cabinet with every patient's individual paperwork in it, and a separate whiteboard in the break room that only shows round numbers — "Clinic 4 saw 310 visits last month." Anyone can look at the whiteboard. Almost nobody gets a key to the filing cabinet.

This video builds the whiteboard. We connect our reporting tool, Power BI, only to the whiteboard-style summary numbers, and we make sure there's no secret hallway from the whiteboard back into the locked filing cabinet. That way, the people allowed to see only round, clinic-level numbers can never accidentally — or on purpose — get back to one patient's private file through the dashboard.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The modeling discipline here is refusing to let Power BI quietly reopen a governance boundary that was deliberately built one layer below it. `claims_summary_gold` is pre-aggregated to clinic and day and contains no patient-level rows at all, which means it needs no row filter and no column mask of its own — the governance already happened upstream, at the grain where PHI actually lives. The job in this lesson is purely to not undo that by giving the report a second path to the row-level table.

We connect in Import mode, not DirectQuery: `claims_summary_gold` refreshes once a night, after the Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline and the Databricks Workflow that orchestrates it finish, so there's no freshness argument for querying live, only added query cost. Every DAX measure is a thin pass-through of a column the gold table already computed — `SUM(total_billed_amount)`, not a measure that re-derives what counts as billed from row-level claims, because this report has no row-level claims to re-derive anything from in the first place. That absence is the actual control. Rolling the daily grain up to a monthly trend is a job for a calendar dimension, not for a baked-in month column on the gold table — the same `dim_date`-style modeling used for trend reporting throughout this path.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm exactly what this report is allowed to touch

Before opening Power BI, write down the one table this report may query and why it's safe to summarize network-wide:

```
TABLE:  harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
GRAIN:  one row per clinic, per service_date (day)
COLUMNS: clinic_id, service_date, claim_count, total_billed_amount,
         denied_claim_count
CONTAINS NO: patient_id, patient_name, patient_ssn --
         neither column tagged pii_category = 'phi' on
         claims_detail_gold exists in this table at all.
```

This table needs no row filter and no column mask of its own — it was never given patient-level rows to protect in the first place. That's the entire reason it's the one safe to point a cross-clinic dashboard at.

## Step 2 — Connect in Import mode, timed against the real refresh schedule

The Databricks Workflow that orchestrates Auto Loader ingestion, the Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline, and the gold refresh finishes its nightly run by 4:00am. In Power BI Desktop: **Get Data → Databricks**, point at the SQL warehouse, select only `claims_summary_gold`, a small `dim_clinic` table (clinic_id, clinic_name, region), and a standard `dim_date` calendar table. Leave connectivity on **Import**, not DirectQuery, and schedule the Power BI service refresh for 6:00am — two hours of buffer past the pipeline's finish time, the same backward-planning logic used for the nightly batch window earlier in this series.

## Step 3 — Build the smallest model that answers the question

```
dim_clinic[clinic_id]  1 ───── *  claims_summary_gold[clinic_id]
dim_date[date_key]     1 ───── *  claims_summary_gold[service_date]
```

Single direction, filtering outward from both dimensions. `dim_date` is what turns this daily-grain table into a monthly trend view -- the month rollup happens in the model, not as a baked-in column on the gold table. There is no second fact table to relate this to — resist the urge to add anything from `claims_detail_gold` "just for one more field." If a future request genuinely needs row-level detail, that's a new, separately governed report, not an addition to this model.

## Step 4 — Write measures that quote the gold table, not reinterpret it

```dax
Total Billed =
SUM ( claims_summary_gold[total_billed_amount] )

Claim Count =
SUM ( claims_summary_gold[claim_count] )

Denial Rate =
DIVIDE ( SUM ( claims_summary_gold[denied_claim_count] ),
         SUM ( claims_summary_gold[claim_count] ), 0 )
```

Every measure aggregates a column the gold table already computed. None of them recomputes what counts as "billed" or "denied" from row-level claims data this report was never given access to.

## Step 5 — Validate a real number before publishing anything

Pick the clinic and month affected by the negative-claims bug fixed two lessons ago and confirm the card matches a direct query, summing the daily grain by hand the way Power BI's date table does automatically:

```sql
SELECT SUM(total_billed_amount) AS july_total
FROM harborview.gold.claims_summary_gold
WHERE clinic_id = 'CLN-04'
  AND service_date BETWEEN '2026-07-01' AND '2026-07-31';
-- $186,420.00 -- post-backfill figure
```

If the Power BI card doesn't match this number to the cent, the model itself — a relationship direction, an unwanted filter — is altering the figure before anyone sees it, and that gets fixed before this goes to a single stakeholder.

## Step 6 — Enforce the boundary technically, not just by convention

Don't rely on nobody adding `claims_detail_gold` to the model later. Grant the Power BI service principal `SELECT` on `claims_summary_gold` and `dim_clinic` only — no grant at all on `claims_detail_gold` — so the boundary holds even if someone tries to extend this report six months from now without reading this lesson first.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Connected Power BI to claims_summary_gold only, Import mode, refreshing at 6am after the nightly pipeline finishes. Every measure is a straight aggregation of a gold-table column — no DAX re-derives billed, paid, or denial logic from row-level data. Validated the Clinic 04 July total against a direct query before publishing, and the Power BI service principal has no SELECT grant on claims_detail_gold at all, so the boundary is enforced by Unity Catalog, not just by nobody adding the table to the model.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Clinical leadership and Finance now have one dashboard for cross-clinic trends, built only on the aggregated numbers — it has no way to show one patient's record even if someone tried to extend it later. That's a real technical guarantee, not just a design intention.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Your leadership team now has one trend dashboard across all 15 clinics, and it's built so it physically cannot expose an individual patient's information — the dashboard only has access to the summarized numbers, nothing more granular. That protection is enforced by the platform itself, not by hoping nobody misuses it.

lessons.title: Presenting the New Access Model to Compliance and Clinical Teams
lessons.summary: The real meeting: walking Compliance and Clinical Quality through the clinic row filters and identifier masks together, and telling them honestly about the warn-severity bug that let negative claim amounts through.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the meeting the governance work in this series has been building toward: Harborview's Compliance officer and the Clinical Quality lead, in one room, seeing the new Unity Catalog access model on `claims_detail_gold` for the first time, together. It does not stay comfortable the whole time — the presentation also has to cover the expectation that ran at "warn" severity for six weeks and let negative-amount claim rows through into the gold layer, quietly understating one clinic-month's billed total before anyone caught it.

The skill here isn't building anything new. It's presenting a real access control, demonstrated live, right alongside a real mistake — found, explained honestly, and already fixed — instead of presenting only the parts of the build that make the project look flawless.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you built a new lock for your family's filing cabinet, and while you're showing everyone how the new lock works, you also have to admit that the old lock had a loose screw for a few weeks that let one drawer pop open by accident — nothing valuable got taken, but it could have. The right move isn't to hide that from the people who trusted you with the cabinet. It's to show them the new lock working, explain exactly what went wrong with the old one, and show them what you changed so a loose screw like that gets caught a lot faster next time.

That's this meeting — showing off the real protection that's now in place, and being straight about the real mistake that happened before it was fully locked down.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The structure that makes this meeting work is presenting the access model as a live demonstration, not a slide describing it, and keeping the governance story and the bug story as two separate pieces of honesty rather than blurring them into one vague "things are more secure now" narrative. The row filter and column mask are things you can show running — log in as a clinic-assigned analyst, query `claims_detail_gold`, and the result set is already limited to that analyst's clinic with the patient name and SSN columns coming back redacted, no application-level trust required.

The bug deserves its own honest telling, including why "warn" severity was a defensible choice at the time: at pipeline go-live, the team didn't yet know whether every negative `billed_amount` was an error, or whether some were a legitimate payer-side adjustment line that would have been wrongly destroyed by a stricter rule before anyone understood the real pattern. Choosing to log and let the ambiguous rows through, rather than silently dropping data that might have been valid, was a reasonable call under that uncertainty — it just turned out, once the actual pattern (duplicate reversal rows from a payer correction file) was understood, that drop was the right severity after all. Naming that reasoning, instead of either over-apologizing or glossing over it, is what makes the explanation land as competent rather than careless.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Prepare a live demonstration, not a slide about the access model

Before the meeting, set up two real query sessions to run side by side: one logged in as a `billing_analysts` member assigned to Clinic 04 (restricted by the row filter), one as a `compliance_team` member (network-wide, unmasked). Have both ready to run against `claims_detail_gold` the moment the meeting starts.

## Step 2 — Open with the access model working, live, before mentioning any bug

```sql
-- As a billing_analysts member assigned to Clinic 04:
SELECT clinic_id, patient_name, patient_ssn, billed_amount
FROM harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
LIMIT 5;
-- Every row: clinic_id = 'CLN-04'. patient_name / patient_ssn: NULL.

-- As a compliance_team member, same query:
-- Rows span all 15 clinics. patient_name / patient_ssn: unmasked.
```

Showing the row filter and the mask actually running, with two real logins, earns far more trust than describing them.

## Step 3 — Name the bug plainly, with the real mechanism and the real number

```
WHAT HAPPENED: a data-quality expectation on billed_amount
  (expect_or_warn: "billed_amount >= 0") was set to WARN severity,
  not DROP. For about six weeks, 212 claim rows carrying a negative
  billed_amount -- duplicate reversal entries from a payer correction
  file -- logged a violation but were still written through to
  claims_clean and on into claims_summary_gold.

REAL IMPACT: Clinic 04's July total_billed_amount came in roughly
  $9,400 lower than it should have, against a monthly total for that
  clinic of about $186,420 after the fix -- a real distortion, caught
  before it reached a stakeholder report, not a catastrophic one.
```

## Step 4 — Explain honestly why WARN seemed like the right call at the time

```
"When this pipeline went live, we didn't yet know whether every
negative claim amount was a data error, or whether some were a
legitimate adjustment line from a payer. Choosing WARN -- log it,
but don't silently destroy data that might be valid -- was a
reasonable way to avoid dropping real claims before we understood
the actual pattern. Once we looked closely and confirmed these were
duplicate reversal rows, not legitimate adjustments, DROP was clearly
the right call -- that's exactly what changed."
```

## Step 5 — Show what's in place now, not just that it's "fixed"

```
- Expectation changed from expect_or_warn to expect_or_drop on
  billed_amount >= 0.
- The affected six-week window was re-run through the pipeline
  (backfill), correcting claims_summary_gold in place.
- Every expectation's violation counts, for every pipeline run, now
  feed a small dashboard the data engineering team reviews weekly --
  not just this one rule, all of them.
```

## Step 6 — Rehearse the two hard questions before the room asks them

```
Q: "Could a bug like this have exposed PHI instead of just a dollar
    figure?"
A: "This specific bug was about a billed amount, not patient
    identifiers -- it never touched the row filter or the masks
    you just saw running. But it's a fair question, which is why
    we're now watching every expectation's violation counts, not
    assuming a WARN rule is harmless just because this one was."

Q: "How do we know the row filter and the masks themselves don't
    have a similar gap?"
A: "They're enforced by Unity Catalog on the table itself, not by
    application code -- there's no code path that can query this
    table and skip them, which is a different and stronger
    guarantee than a data-quality rule that merely logs."
```

## Step 7 — Close with explicit, written acknowledgment

Ask both Compliance and Clinical Quality to confirm in writing that they've seen the access model demonstrated and understand the billed-amount finding and its fix. This isn't paperwork for its own sake — it's the same sign-off discipline used throughout this series, and it's what you point back to later if either team's understanding of this access model is ever questioned.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran the access-model walkthrough live for Compliance and Clinical Quality — two real logins side by side showed the clinic row filter and the name/SSN mask actually enforcing, not just described. Named the billed-amount WARN-severity finding directly: 212 negative-amount rows, roughly $9,400 understated on Clinic 04's July total, root-caused to duplicate payer reversal rows, now fixed to DROP severity with a weekly-reviewed violation-count dashboard across every expectation in the pipeline.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Got Compliance and Clinical Quality in the same room to see the new access controls working firsthand, and we were upfront about a real data-quality finding from earlier in the build rather than letting them hear about it secondhand. Both teams signed off in writing on the access model and the explanation.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Compliance and your clinical quality team have now seen, live, exactly how patient data is protected clinic by clinic. We also told them plainly about a billing-total error we found and already fixed — a small one, caught before it reached anyone's report — because getting ahead of that kind of finding is what keeps trust intact.

lessons.title: Writing the Handoff Docs: Data Classification, Access Policy, and Lineage
lessons.summary: Three documents that let this platform survive without you standing next to it: a classification reference, a plain-English access policy, and a lineage description in prose.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The access model is built, demonstrated, and signed off — now it needs to survive a staff turnover, an auditor's question, or a new analyst's first week without you in the room to explain it. This video writes the three documents that make that possible: a data classification reference stating exactly which columns in `claims_detail_gold` are tagged `pii_category = 'phi'` and why; a plain-English access-policy document describing who sees what and why, in sentences a Compliance officer can read without a Unity Catalog manual; and a lineage description in prose, tracing one claim from the file that lands on disk to the Power BI card a clinical leader reads months from now.

These three documents answer three different questions. Classification answers "is this specific column sensitive, and how sensitive." Access policy answers "who is allowed to see it, and on what basis." Lineage answers "where did this specific number actually come from." A platform that can only answer these questions by someone remembering the answer isn't actually handed off.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you organize a huge shared toy box for a daycare, with some toys marked "little kids only" and some marked "everyone." For this to actually work once you're not standing there, you need three things written down: a list of which toys are marked which way and why, a note explaining which helper is allowed to hand out which toys, and a simple story of how a toy gets from the delivery truck into the box in the first place. Without all three written down, the next helper who shows up has to guess — and guessing is exactly how a "little kids only" toy ends up somewhere it shouldn't.

That's what this video writes down for Harborview's claims data.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The classification reference and the access-policy document are deliberately separate artifacts because they answer different audiences' different questions, and conflating them produces a document that satisfies neither. Classification is a column-level, almost mechanical fact — this column is tagged PHI, for this reason — and belongs as close to the data as possible, which is why it's written as Unity Catalog column tags, queryable by anyone with Catalog Explorer access, not just prose in a shared drive. Access policy is a role-level, human-readable narrative — a clinic analyst sees their clinic's rows with identifiers masked, a Compliance officer sees everything unmasked for audit purposes — and deliberately contains no SQL, because its reader is a Compliance officer or a new hire, not a developer debugging a grant.

The lineage description does a third job neither of the others does: it answers "where did this number come from" in a way a person can follow without opening Catalog Explorer's lineage graph at all, which matters because the graph is excellent for a developer tracing an object and useless for an auditor who wants a sentence they can quote. Writing it in prose, end to end, from the file drop through Auto Loader, through the Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline's expectations, into the gold tables, and out to Power BI, is what turns a correct pipeline into a pipeline someone outside the data team can actually explain back.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Write the data classification reference as column tags, not just prose

```sql
ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
ALTER COLUMN patient_name SET TAGS ('pii_category' = 'phi');

ALTER TABLE harborview.gold.claims_detail_gold
ALTER COLUMN patient_ssn SET TAGS ('pii_category' = 'phi');
```

```
CLASSIFICATION REFERENCE -- claims_detail_gold

COLUMN             TAG            WHY
patient_name       phi            Direct identifier.
patient_ssn         phi            Direct identifier; the column the
                                   column mask protects, and the
                                   highest-sensitivity field in the table.

claim_id, clinic_id, service_date, billed_amount -- NOT tagged phi.
Financial and operational fields, not health information tied to an
identifiable individual on their own.
```

Tagging these at the column level means anyone with Catalog Explorer access can filter by classification directly, instead of trusting a document to stay in sync with the actual table.

## Step 2 — Write the access-policy document in plain English, no SQL

```
HARBORVIEW CLAIMS DATA -- ACCESS POLICY

BILLING_ANALYSTS
  See: claims_detail_gold rows for their own assigned clinic only.
  patient_name and patient_ssn return NULL.
  Why: their job is clinic-level claims work, not cross-clinic or
       patient-identity work.

COMPLIANCE_TEAM
  See: claims_detail_gold, all 15 clinics, identifiers unmasked.
  Why: auditing and investigating specific claims requires confirming
       the real patient and claim identity, network-wide.

CLINICAL_QUALITY
  See: claims_detail_gold for their own assigned clinic (patient_name
       and patient_ssn still return NULL); claims_summary_gold across
       all 15 clinics for broader trend work, since that table carries
       no patient-level data to protect in the first place.
  Why: quality review needs clinic-level claim detail and network-wide
       trend context, but never needs to know who a patient is.

FINANCE AND CLINICAL LEADERSHIP
  See: claims_summary_gold only -- clinic and day totals, no
       patient-level rows exist in this table at all.
  Why: trend reporting needs totals, never an individual claim.

HOW THIS IS ENFORCED: a row filter checks each querying user's clinic
assignment against the clinic_access_lookup table before returning any
row. Column masks check the requester's group membership before
showing patient_name or patient_ssn in the clear. Neither depends on
the report or the person querying to self-police -- both run on the
table itself.
```

## Step 3 — Write the lineage description as a paragraph, not just a diagram

```
Each clinic's claims arrive as a daily file dropped into a cloud
storage landing path by the clearinghouse. Auto Loader picks up new
files incrementally and lands them, largely as-is, in
harborview.bronze.claims_raw. A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline reads
from there, applies data-quality expectations -- including the
billed-amount check that now drops rather than warns -- and writes
the cleaned result to harborview.silver.claims_clean. From silver,
the gold layer is built two ways: claims_summary_gold aggregates to
clinic and day for trend reporting, and
claims_detail_gold keeps the row-level claims, protected by the row
filter and column masks described above. A nightly Databricks
Workflow orchestrates every one of those steps in order; Power BI
connects only to claims_summary_gold, refreshing each morning after
that Workflow completes.
```

## Step 4 — Put all three documents where the next person will actually find them

Commit the column tags directly on the table (they're permanent and queryable). Put the access-policy document and the lineage paragraph in Harborview's shared compliance documentation space, not a personal drive, and add a Catalog Explorer comment on `claims_detail_gold` itself linking to both — so someone who finds the table first, before finding any document, still finds their way to the policy.

## Step 5 — Walk one person from Compliance through finding all three, live

Spend fifteen minutes showing a Compliance representative exactly how to filter Catalog Explorer by the `phi` tag, where the access-policy document lives, and how to read the lineage paragraph against the real pipeline. A document nobody was shown how to find is a handoff in name only.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Tagged patient_name and patient_ssn as pii_category = phi directly on claims_detail_gold, wrote the plain-English access-policy doc covering billing_analysts, compliance_team, clinical_quality, and leadership separately, and wrote the end-to-end lineage from the clearinghouse file drop through Auto Loader, the Lakeflow pipeline's expectations, silver, both gold tables, and the nightly Workflow, out to Power BI. All three live in Harborview's shared compliance space with a Catalog Explorer comment pointing to them.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've documented not just how the pipeline runs, but exactly which columns are sensitive and why, who's allowed to see what, and where every number traces back to. That means a new analyst, an auditor, or a staff change doesn't depend on someone remembering the answer.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've written down, in plain language, exactly what's sensitive in this data, who's allowed to see it, and how a number on a report traces all the way back to the original claims file. That's what makes this handoff real rather than just a project that quietly depends on one person's memory.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Changed, and What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the whole Harborview build — what's genuinely governed and running, and what's still manual, fragile, or a single point of failure.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and it isn't a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Harborview Health Partners went from a shared-login, no-governance claims setup to a real pipeline: Auto Loader ingestion, a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline enforcing data-quality expectations, a medallion-architecture gold layer, Unity Catalog row filters and column masks protecting patient-level data by clinic, classification tags marking exactly what's sensitive, Databricks Workflows orchestrating all of it nightly, and a Power BI report that reads only the governed, aggregated numbers. A real bug — a WARN-severity expectation that let negative claim amounts through — was found, explained honestly to Compliance and Clinical Quality, fixed, and backfilled. That part is real, and it's done.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what's still manual, still fragile, or still a single point of failure, so whoever maintains this platform next — quite possibly you, six months from now — isn't caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months building a really solid new filing system for a busy office — locked drawers, clear labels, a sign-out sheet for who's allowed to see what. It's genuinely good. But a good builder doesn't just say "it's perfect, goodbye" — they say "this part is solid, but someone still has to update the list of who works where, and if the delivery truck ever drops off a totally new kind of paperwork, someone has to notice and decide where it's allowed to go." That honesty is what keeps the filing system safe to keep using, instead of someone discovering its limits the hard way, during an audit, six months from now.

That's this whole video: being straight about what's genuinely solid in what we built for Harborview, and what still needs a human checking in on it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most wrap-ups skip: it states the real architecture plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what's running, and it enumerates the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the billed-amount bug — not "there's room for improvement," but named, concrete limitations. For Harborview, three are worth stating without softening: expectation violations outside the one rule that got escalated to DROP severity still only surface on a dashboard a human has to open and read, not an alert that pages anyone, which means a new data-quality problem can sit quietly in the pipeline's logs for days before someone notices; the clinic row filter is only as current as the `clinic_access_lookup` table underneath it, and nothing in the pipeline detects when that table has drifted from reality — a clinic transfer or a departure updates access only when a person remembers to edit the lookup table, not automatically; and Auto Loader's schema evolution, which is exactly what makes nightly ingestion resilient to a clearinghouse adding a column, has no governance gate attached to it — a new column lands in bronze and can flow downstream before anyone has decided whether it's PHI, needs a mask, or needs a row filter.

Naming these isn't an admission of failure — overselling a governed system's completeness to Compliance is itself the exact category of trust problem this series spent two lessons ago fixing honestly. The honest version of "done" is "this solved the real governance problem we scoped, found and fixed a real bug along the way, and here are its real edges, named for whoever picks this up next."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — State the finished architecture in one pass, end to end

```
SOURCE:        Daily claims file per clinic, dropped by the clearinghouse
INGESTION:     Auto Loader, incremental, into harborview.bronze.claims_raw
```
