```
TRANSFORM:     Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline, enforcing data-quality
               expectations (billed_amount >= 0 now at DROP severity)
               -> harborview.silver.claims_clean
GOLD:          claims_summary_gold (clinic and day, aggregated)
               claims_detail_gold (row-level, governed)
GOVERNED BY:   Unity Catalog row filters (clinic-based access) and
               column masks (patient_name, patient_ssn) on
               claims_detail_gold; pii_category = 'phi' classification
               tags on every sensitive column
ORCHESTRATED:  A Databricks Workflow, nightly, running ingestion through
               gold refresh in order
SURFACED IN:   One Power BI report, Import mode, reading
               claims_summary_gold only -- never the row-level table
DOCUMENTED BY: A classification reference, a plain-English access
               policy, and an end-to-end lineage description
```

Every box in that chain was built, demonstrated to Compliance and Clinical Quality, and is now running -- that's the real, defensible claim this project gets to make.

## Step 2 — Name what's still manual, specifically

```
GAP 1: Expectation violations still need a human looking at a dashboard.
  Only the billed_amount rule was escalated to DROP severity after the
  investigation two lessons ago. Every other expectation in the
  pipeline still logs violations that feed a dashboard the data
  engineering team reviews weekly -- nothing pages anyone between
  reviews. A new, unnoticed data-quality problem can sit in the logs
  for days before a human opens that dashboard and looks.

GAP 2: The clinic-assignment lookup table needs a manual process to
  stay current. The row filter on claims_detail_gold is only as
  correct as clinic_access_lookup, and nothing in the pipeline checks
  that table against Harborview's actual staffing. When someone
  transfers clinics or leaves, their access changes only when a human
  remembers to update that one table -- a real, if narrow, path to
  stale access.

GAP 3: Auto Loader's schema evolution has no governance gate attached.
  The same schema evolution that makes nightly ingestion resilient to
  a clearinghouse adding a column also means a genuinely new column --
  a new diagnosis field, a new identifier -- lands in bronze
  automatically, before anyone has decided whether it's PHI, needs a
  mask, or needs a row filter. Resilience and a governance decision
  are not the same thing, and right now only the first one is automatic.
```

## Step 3 — Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
"This project replaced a shared-login, no-governance claims setup
with a real pipeline enforcing clinic-based row filters, identifier
masking, and data-quality expectations, and found and fixed a real
bug that had been understating a billing total. It did not add
alerting beyond a weekly-reviewed dashboard, an automated check on
the clinic-access lookup table, or a governance gate on new columns
arriving through schema evolution -- those are real, named gaps for
a future phase, not oversights we're pretending don't exist."
```

## Step 4 — Leave a short, prioritized list for "if there's a phase two"

```
1. Real alerting -- not just a weekly dashboard -- on every data-
   quality expectation, not only the one that already caused a
   problem. Closes Gap 1, highest value for the lowest lift.
2. A recurring, at least partly automated reconciliation of
   clinic_access_lookup against Harborview's actual staffing records.
   Closes Gap 2.
3. A review step -- even a simple one -- that a human must clear
   before a schema-evolution-added column is allowed to reach a gold
   table ungoverned. Closes Gap 3, the hardest and most structural
   of the three.
```

That's the real, unglamorous ending: not every problem solved, but every remaining one named, owned, and ready to hand to whoever picks this up next -- the same honesty this series used two lessons ago when a bug, not just a success, was the thing being presented.
